ii  
 
CERTIFICATE OF QUALIFIED PERSON – ADRIAN RALPH  
I, Adrian Ralph, FAusIMM, as an author of the report entitled “Technical Report, Nyanzaga Gold Project 
Feasibility Study – Tanzania” (the “Report”) prepared for Perseus Mining Limited (“Perseus”) and with an 
effective date of April 28, 2025, do hereby state: 
a) I am employed as General Manager Technical Services and Studies by Perseus of Level 2, 437 Roberts 
Road, Subiaco, Western Australia. 
b) I graduated with a Bachelor of Engineering in Mining Engineering from the Western Australian School 
of Mines in 2001. I completed a Master of Science in Mineral Economics from the Western Australian School 
of Mines in 2011. 
c) I am a registered Fellow of the Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy (#301892). I have 
worked as a mining engineer, in the mining industry for a total of 24 years since my graduation. My relevant 
experience for the purpose of the Report is prior experience as a Project Manager and Mining Manager for 
both Open Pit and Underground Operations, and as a Study Manager, Principal Consultant and General 
Manager of Technical Services and Studies for mining projects in Australia, Africa, South America and Asia. 
d) I have read the definition of “qualified person” set out in National Instrument 43-101 (Standards of 
Disclosure for Mineral Projects) (the “Instrument”) and certify that by reason of my education, affiliation with 
a professional association (as defined in the Instrument) and past relevant work experience, I fulfil the 
requirements to be a “qualified person” for the purposes of the Instrument. 
e) I have visited Nyanzaga Gold Project site in May 2024. The purpose of the visits was as manager of 
the Nyanzaga Gold Project Feasibility Study in my roles as General Manager Technical Services and Studies, 
as an employee of Perseus Mining. 
f) I am responsible for Sections 1.1, 1.11-1.12, 1.16, 1.19-1.20, 15-16, 20 and 23-27 of the Report. 
g) I am not independent of Perseus pursuant to Section 1.5 of the Instrument. 
h) I have read the Instrument and the sections of the Report for which I am responsible and which have 
been prepared in compliance with the Instrument. 
i) My involvement with the Nyanzaga Gold Project is limited to my work as an employee of Perseus, 
commencing August 2021.  
j) At the effective date of the Report, to the best of my knowledge, information and belief, the sections 
of the Report I am responsible for contain all scientific and technical information that is required to be 
disclosed to make the Report not misleading. 
 
Dated this 10th day of June 2025 at Perth, Western Australia. 
 
 
 
Adrian Ralph, BEng (Mining), MSc (Mineral Economics), FAusIMM

TECHNICAL REPORT  
iii  
 
CERTIFICATE OF QUALIFIED PERSON – DANIEL SAUNDERS  
I, Daniel Richard Saunders, FAusIMM, as an author of the report entitled “Technical Report, Nyanzaga Gold 
Project Feasibility Study – Tanzania” (the “Report”) prepared for Perseus Mining Limited (“Perseus”) and with 
an effective date of April 28, 2025, do hereby state: 
a) I am employed as Group Resource Geologist Business Growth by Perseus of Level 2, 437 Roberts 
Road, Subiaco, Western Australia. 
b) I graduated with a Bachelor of Science in Mineral Exploration and Mining Geology from the Western 
Australian School of Mines in 1999. I completed a Graduate Certificate in Mine Planning and Design at Curtin 
University, Western Australia in 2009, and a Graduate Certificate in Geostatistics at Edith Cowan University, 
Western Australia in 2014. 
c) I am a registered Fellow of the Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy (# 220021). I have 
been practicing my profession continuously since 1999 and my experience covers 2 6 years in the mining 
industry involving exploration, development, production, resource evaluation, geological consulting  and 
corporate technical roles working on projects in Australia, Africa, South America, North America and Asia. 
d) I have read the definition of “qualified person” set out in National Instrument 43-101 (Standards of 
Disclosure for Mineral Projects) (the “Instrument”) and certify that by reason of my education, affiliation with 
a professional association (as defined in the Instrument) and past relevant work experience, I fulfil the 
requirements to be a “qualified person” for the purposes of the Instrument. 
e) I visited the Nyanzaga Gold Project in May 2024, during September and October 2024, and in March 
2025. The purpose of the visit was to review drilling and sampling practices, data collection and validation, 
analytical laboratory assessment, and review of the project geology in my role as Group Geologist – Business 
Growth. 
f) I am responsible for Sections 1.2-1.8, 1.10, 2-12, and 14 of the Report. 
g) I am not independent of Perseus pursuant to Section 1.5 of the Instrument. 
h) I have read the Instrument and the sections of the Report for which I am responsible and which have 
been prepared in compliance with the Instrument. 
i) My involvement with the Nyanzaga Gold Project is limited to my work as an employee of Perseus, 
commencing August 2023. 
j) At the effective date of the Report, to the best of my knowledge, information and belief, the sections 
of the Report I am responsible for contain all scientific and technical information that is required to be 
disclosed to make the Report not misleading. 
 
Dated this 10th day of June 2025 at Perth, Western Australia. 
 
 
 
 
Daniel Saunders, BSc, FAusIMM

TECHNICAL REPORT  
iv  
 
CERTIFICATE OF QUALIFIED PERSON – BENJAMIN STRONG  
I, Benjamin David Strong, FAusIMM, as an author of the report entitled “Technical Report, Nyanzaga Gold 
Project Feasibility Study – Tanzania” (the “Report”) prepared for Perseus Mining Limited (“Perseus”) and with 
an effective date of April 28, 2025, do hereby state: 
a) I am employed as Group Manager Processing, Infrastructure and Tailings by Perseus of Level 2, 437 
Roberts Road, Subiaco, Western Australia. 
b) I graduated with a Bachelor of Science in Extractive Metallurgy from the Western Australian School 
of Mines (Curtin University of Technology) in 2008. 
c) I am a registered Fellow of the Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy (# 208858). I have 
worked as a metallurgist and process engineer  in the mining industry for a total of 16 years since my 
graduation. My relevant experience in the mining industry involving roles in process plant operations, 
process plant commissioning, extractive metallurgy, test work program management, process engineering 
and plant design, study management, business management, financial modelling and corporate technical 
coordination and management, predominantly related to gold processing plants . This experience covers 
operations and projects in Africa, Australia, Asia, North America and South America. 
d) I have read the definition of “qualified person” set out in National Instrument 43-101 (Standards of 
Disclosure for Mineral Projects) (the “Instrument”) and certify that by reason of my education, affiliation with 
a professional association (as defined in the Instrument) and past relevant work experience, I fulfil the 
requirements to be a “qualified person” for the purposes of the Instrument. 
e) I have visited the Nyanzaga Gold Project site from March 15 to March 20, 2025. The purpose of the 
visit was to provide support to and conduct activities as part of the Nyanzaga Gold Project Feasibility Study 
in my role as Group Manager Processing, Infrastructure and Tailings, as an employee of Perseus Mining. 
f) I am responsible for Sections 1.9, 1.13-1.15, 1.17-1.18, 13, 17-19 and 21-22 of the Report. 
g) I am not independent of Perseus pursuant to Section 1.5 of the Instrument. 
h) I have read the Instrument and the sections of the Report for which I am responsible and which have 
been prepared in compliance with the Instrument. 
i) My involvement with the Nyanzaga Gold Project is limited to my work as an employee of Perseus, 
commencing February 2023. 
j) At the effective date of the Report, to the best of my knowledge, information and belief, the sections 
of the Report I am responsible for contain all scientific and technical information that is required to be 
disclosed to make the Report not misleading. 
 
Dated this 10th day of June 2025 at Perth, Western Australia. 
 
 
 
Benjamin Strong, BSc (Extractive Metallurgy), FAusIMM

1. SUMMARY  
1.1 INTRODUCTION, LOCATION AND OWNERSHIP 
This report, entitled the “Technical Report, Nyanzaga Gold Project Feasibility Study – Tanzania” (the Report), 
was prepared by Perseus Mining Limited (Perseus or the Company). Perseus is a Producing Issuer, as defined 
in the Canadian Securities Administrator’s National Instrument 43-101 - Standards of Disclosure for Mineral 
Projects (NI 43-101). The Report complies with the requirements of NI 43-101.  
The Report was prepared to align with the Company’s continuous disclosure of exploration results, Mineral 
Resources and Mineral Reserves in accordance with NI 43-101 and the 2012 Australasian Code for Reporting 
of Exploration Results, Mineral Resources and Ore Reserves (the JORC Code). The effective date of this Report 
is April 28, 2025 (the Effective Date). 
Specifically, the objective of this Report is to summarise the results of the Nyanzaga Gold Project Feasibility 
Study (the Feasibility Study) to demonstrate the technical and economic viability of developing an open pit 
mining operation at the Nyanzaga Gold Project. 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project (the Project) is located in north-western Tanzania, south of Lake Victoria within 
the Sengerema District of the Mwanza Region. The Project is approximately 60 km southwest of Mwanza 
(Tanzania’s second largest city) and 7 km southeast of Ngoma. 
Perseus acquired the Project in the second quarter of 2024 via the acquisition of OreCorp Limited (OreCorp). 
The Project comprises a single 23.36 km2 Special Mining Lease (SML 653/2021) that covers the proposed 
development area, nine granted prospecting licences and one prospecting licence application covering an 
additional 163.93 km2. 
The Company’s interest in SML 653/2021 is held via 80% owned Tanzanian subsidiary Nyanzaga Mining 
Corporation Limited (NMCL). The remaining 20% of NMCL is owned by the Government of Tanzania.  
1.2 HISTORY 
The exploration history of the Nyanzaga gold deposit dates to the colonial period when gossan outcrops were 
identified on Tusker Hill in 1937. Modern exploration commenced in 1996 involving mapping, soil sampling, 
rock chip sampling, geophysical surveys, and drilling programs. These activities were conducted by various 
companies until 2015 when OreCorp entered the Project via a joint venture with Acacia Mining plc. 
OreCorp commenced a systematic relogging program of existing drilling to build a consistent reference for 
subsequent geological and structural interpretations, along with a range of other exploration and resource 
definition activities. 
A Mineral Resource Estimate (MRE) for Nyanzaga and the adjacent satellite deposit Kilimani was completed 
by CSA Global in March 2017 and updated in September 2017. The September 2017 MRE for Nyanzaga was 
used as the basis for the OreCorp Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) released in August 2022. 
Following acquisition of the Project in 2024 Perseus initiated various studies aimed at updating the DFS 
reported by OreCorp with consideration of a change in operating methodology from a small open pit and 
underground operation (proposed by OreCorp) to a larger open pit only scenario.  
1.3 GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND MINERALISATION 
The Nyanzaga Project is located on the north-eastern flank of the Sukumaland Greenstone Belt, representing 
one of the six greenstone belts within the Tanzanian portion of the Lake Victoria Goldfield. The greenstone 
belts contain a diverse sequence of volca nic and sedimentary rocks of mostly greenschist metamorphic 
grade, which host numerous gold prospects and active mines (e.g., Bulyanhulu, Geita, and North Mara). The 
greenstone sequences within these belts have been divided into the Nyanzian Supergroup (Nyanzian) and 
Kavirondian Supergroup (Kavirondian).

Further division of the Nyanzian has been proposed into a “Lower Series” of mafic -intermediate volcanic 
(minor ultramafic) with subordinate iron formations and clastic sediments, and an “Upper Series” of felsic to 
intermediate volcanics, volcaniclastics, iron formations, chert, mudstone, and sandstones. The Kavirondian, 
which unconformably overlies the Nyanzian, is dominated by coarse clastic sediments (sandstones and 
conglomerates). 
The Project is situated on the north -eastern flank of the Sukumaland Greenstone Belt. Rock sequences 
comprise Nyanzian-aged sequences of mafic volcanics in the far south -west and banded -iron-formation, 
tuffs, mudstone, sandstone and epiclastics of general volcanogenic origin and massive sulfide lenses and 
volcanics of rhyodacitic to andesitic composition. The sequences are tightly folded and strike generally west-
northwest. 
In the central part of the project, the Nyanzaga and Kilimani groups are defined. The Nyanzaga Group is 
divided into a sequence of three broad mappable units from drill core and outcrop mapping. These units are 
folded into the north-northwest plunging Nyanzaga Anticline. These sequences are in turn overlain by the 
Kilimani Group which appears to be tectonically dislocated from the underlying Nyanzaga Group by faulting 
and potential earlier thrusts. 
The Kilimani deposit, located 450 m northeast of Nyanzaga, is developed in the fold hinge of an interpreted 
double plunging anticline. The bulk of the defined deposit occurs in the heavily weathered, upper 140 m from 
surface. 
A series of different faulting sets has been recognised across the Nyanzaga project area. These include 
observed outcrop positions with suggested sinistral movement; others with inferred dextral movement; a 
series of steep faults sub -parallel to bedding; and several low angle thrust faults. Additionally, east-west 
trending normal faults with minor displacement have been identified. 
The Nyanzaga and Kilimani mineralisation systems show similar alteration and mineralisation styles, though 
the Kilimani deposit is interpreted to have been emplaced at shallower levels than at Nyanzaga. Typical 
alteration features include pervasive carbonate alteration, varying from distal ferroan-calcite to proximal 
ankerite - sericite dominated and quartz-pyrite alteration. 
The current interpretation indicates that there is a distinct lithological control and most of the gold appears 
to be hosted by iron rich sediments in the form of an extensive stock-work of carbonate, quartz veins, and 
quartz-carbonate breccias. Preferential grade enhancement occurs in selected altered units such as the thick 
cherts, silica-dolomite altered medium grained sandstones, brecciated silica-carbonate altered mudstones; 
or in the late quartz veins as free gold. High-gold grades occur in narrow 5 to 20 mm wide tensional quartz 
veins that developed as conjugate sets and dip moderately to the southwest and southeast. Evidence 
suggests these veins may have developed along the axis of plunging parasitic folds in the area of the cherts; 
or with an apparent pr eference for developing in dolomitised and silicified, medium to coarse grained 
sandstone host rocks. 
1.4 DEPOSIT TYPES 
The Lake Victoria Gold Field hosts numerous small-scale and several large-scale orogenic gold deposits. The 
orogenic deposits are found in regionally metamorphosed terrains of volcanic or sedimentary rocks, of all 
ages from the mid Archaean to the Tertiary. At the broadest scale the deposits were formed d uring 
compressional or transpressional deformation processes at convergent plate margins in accretionary and 
collisional orogenic events, which are typified by the emplacement of abundant granitoid plutons and 
batholiths. In both tectonic regimes, hydrated  marine sedimentary sequences are added to continental 
margins. Subduction related thermal events then drive extensive hydrothermal fluid systems resulting in the 
emplacement of gold bearing quartz veins from depths of 15 km-20 km to surface. 
Orogenic deposits may be subdivided into epizonal (<6 km), mesozonal (6-12 km), and hypozonal (>12 km) 
subtypes based on pressure-temperature conditions of ore formation. Most orogenic gold deposits contain 
2 to 5 percent sulfide minerals and have gold/silver ratios from 5 to 10 and gold fineness >900. Pyrite and 
arsenopyrite are the dominant sulfide minerals, whereas pyrrhotite is more important in higher temperature

ores and base metals are not highly anomalous. Alteration intensity, width, and assemblage vary with the 
host rock, but carbonates, sulfides, muscovite, chlorite, K -feldspar, biotite, tourmaline, and albite are 
generally present. Ore fluids were, in most cases, near -neutral pH, slightly reduced, dominated by sulfide 
complexes and CO2 rich, with low to moderate salinities. 
The Nyanzaga mineralisation is a member of the orogenic clan of gold deposits. It is hosted by a sequence of 
chemical and clastic sediments (chert/sandstone/siltstone), and it displays the typical alteration features of 
an orogenic deposit, such as pervasive carbonate alteration, going from distal ferroan calcite dominated to 
proximal ankerite and sericite dominated and quartz-pyrite alteration. There is a distinct lithological control; 
the majority of the gold is hosted by Fe -rich sediments in form of an extensive stock work (crustif orm 
carbonate veins, quartz veins, quartz carbonate breccias). The brittle deformation style allows the 
mineralisation to be classified as epizonal. 
1.5 EXPLORATION 
Exploration activities that have been conducted across the Project area include: 
• Mapping, soil sampling, rock chips, and geophysics during 1996 by Sub Sahara Resources in joint venture 
with Maiden Gold. 
• Soil sampling, rock chips, trenching, and geophysics during 1997 and 1998 by Sub Sahara Resources in 
joint venture with AvGold. 
• Soil sampling, rock chips, trenching, geophysics, and drilling during 1999 to 2001 by Sub Sahara Resources 
in joint venture with Anglovaal Mining Ltd. 
• Rock chip sampling and drilling by Sub Sahara Resources during 2003. 
• Mapping, soil sampling, geophysics, drilling, and petrography during 2004 to 2009 by Sub Sahara 
Resources in joint venture with Barrick Exploration Africa Ltd (BEAL). 
• Drilling campaigns during 2009 to 2010 by BEAL in joint venture with Western Metals/Indago Resources. 
• Drilling by African Barrick Gold Exploration Ltd during the period 2010 to 2015. 
• Various activities by OreCorp via subsidiary Sotta Mining Corporation Limited (SMCL) during the period 
2015 to 2017 including data validation, collation of geological mapping, relogging of historical drilling, 
geological interpretation, topography surveys, geological mapping, reprocessing of geophysical data,

1.6 DRILLING 
Drilling on the various tenements that comprised the Project commenced in 1997. In the period until OreCorp 
acquired the Project in 2015, drilling available to support Mineral Resource estimations included 877 holes 
for approximately 201,580 m. In the period since OreCorp have managed the project, a total of 280 holes for 
approximately 37,980 m have been completed across the Nyanzaga and Kilimani areas. All drill hole collars 
have been surveyed in UTM grid (Arc 1960 datum) and locations are considered reliable to ±0.5 m in each of 
x, y and z directions. 
A combination of poor ground conditions, weathering characteristics and in some instances driller practices 
(i.e., removal of stabiliser rod in coincident clay and high waterflow areas to reduce chances of bogging) have 
influenced the down-hole trajectories in certain areas of the project. 
Deviation caused by strongly magnetic mudstones and pyrrhotite has also been an observed issue in older 
surveys undertaken with a downhole survey probe based on magnetic readings. Gyroscopic tool readings in 
these strata produce a more reliable hole trace, and as such have superseded the magnetic down-hole survey 
probe data where undertaken and have been updated in the database. 
Reverse circulation samples were collected at 1 m intervals in plastic bags and their weight (25 – 35 kg) was 
recorded in a logbook. Wet samples were collected in polythene bags and allowed to air dry before splitting.

4 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
Prior to September 2005, the samples were combined into 3  m composites by taking a 300  g scoop from 
10 – 15 kg 1 m interval, then mixing it with 300  g scoops from each of two adjacent samples. The 1  kg 
composite sample was then submitted for preparation and analysis. Magnetic susceptibility readings were 
taken every metre. 
From 2015 onwards, depending on the drill rig, the sample was split at the cyclone, or the bulk sample was 
passed through a standalone riffle splitter at the drill site to generate the subsample for analysis. A record 
was made at the drill site of the sample identity numbers and corresponding intervals, and cross checked 
against the pre-drilling sample sheet. 
Diamond core holes collared from surface were normally drilled in HQ diameter to the top of fresh rock and 
the core diameter then reduced to NQ or NQ2, depending on the drilling contractor. Pre-collared holes were 
normally drilled NQ or NQ2 diameter from the commencement of coring. 
The core is marked up for orientation and a cutline is marked offset by approximately 2 cm clockwise of the 
bottom of hole orientation line, with the orientation line preserved on the un-sampled half-core and retained 
in the tray. 
The entire hole is sampled with samples collected nominally at 1 m or at geological contacts. Sampling of 
diamond core was completed using a simple brick saw to cut core into equal halves; one half of the core was 
collected for each nominal 1 m interval making sure that the same half was consistently sampled down the 
hole. No sample interval was less than 20 cm or exceed 1.5 m. 
RC sample recoveries were measured by weighing of the entire recovered sample for each metre drilled. Drill 
core recoveries were logged linearly by drill run. Average core recoveries are typically above 90% for all but 
the upper 10 m of the drill holes. 
1.7 SAMPLE PREPARATION, ANALYSIS AND SECURITY 
All samples have been assayed for gold by 50 g fire assay (FA), primarily SGS Mwanza, with additional assaying 
completed at ALS Mwanza. Both laboratories are accredited and considered independent of the Company. 
All drilling campaigns followed routine monitoring of assay quality through the insertion of QAQC samples 
(standards, blanks and duplicates), and immediate re-assaying where results reported for client-submitted 
standards or blanks casted doubts on the accuracy and quality of the analytical process. 
Sample preparation procedures for both core and RC samples analysed by FA have been consistent for all 
drilling that informs the resource estimate: 
• dry at 95°C ± 5°C for 24 h 
• crush the entire sample to -2 mm 
• split to approximately 800-1,000 g 
• pulverise, normally using LM2 disc pulverisers, to 90% passing 75 µm 
• mat roll and dip approximately 300 g subsample into a kraft packet. 
 
RC sample splitting is undertaken at drill sites under the supervision of Company geologists. Sub-samples are 
methodically bagged and transported to a secure location prior to be dispatched for analysis. Core is logged 
and sampled at the Nyanzaga exploration compound, located in the same secure area. 
Half core samples or RC sample splits that are sent for preparation by commercial laboratories are securely 
packed and transported to Mwanza by laboratory personnel. A sample submission form, detailing sample 
number sequences and number of samples, accompanies each shipment of RC samples or core which is 
transported to the commercial assay laboratory. 
Digital assay reports and electronic certificates are emailed by the laboratories to a pre-set list of Company 
recipients.

In the QP’s opinion, sample security is not considered a significant risk to the reliability of Mineral Resource 
estimates at Nyanzaga. 
A consistent QAQC regime has been maintained during drilling by African Barrick Gold and OreCorp:  
• Certified reference materials (CRMs) were inserted as 150-200 g sachets nominally at a ratio of 1:20 
samples of both RC chips and diamond core despatched for assay. CRMs were sourced from a range of 
suppliers and over various grade ranges across the drilling history of the Project. 
• Blank samples, comprising approximately 3 kg of barren granite sourced from a commercial quarry, were 
submitted at a ratio of 1:20 samples despatched. 
• Field duplicates for RC samples were generated from a riffle split of the bulk reject. Diamond core 
duplicates were submitted using either half or quarter core, or from samples from the coarse rejects 
following crushing. 
Quality control samples were inserted in the sample streams prior to sample despatch. 
Assays reported for CRMs and blank samples were routinely checked against tolerance limits when importing 
assays from digital laboratory reports into the acQuire database. Re -assays were requested for entire 
laboratory batches for which more than one CRM or blank failure arose. 
The performances of CRMs and blank samples have been examined in detail. The precision indicated by 
assays of CRMs indicate relatively poor precision, typical of assaying for gold by commercial laboratories. 
CRM assays are spread fairly symmetrically about expected grades, indicating no significant bias. 
Blank samples indicate no significant cross-contamination in samples preparation and assaying processes. 
In the opinion of the QP, the available quality control data are considered sufficient to establish that the 
assay data are free of any biases or other factors that would materially affect confidence in estimates of 
Mineral Resources.

1.9 MINERAL PROCESSING AND METALLURGICAL TESTING 
Metallurgical testing of Nyanzaga Gold Project ore samples has occurred across a range of test work 
programs between 2005 and 2022. Key test work programs were conducted in 2017 and 2022 to select the 
most suitable processing route, determine the plant operating parameters by ore type for the selected 
processing route, and to define key engineering parameters for process plant design. 
Comminution testing determined that oxide ores are between very low competency to competent, are 
between very soft and hard, and are between non-abrasive and abrasive; and fresh ores are between low 
competency to very competent, are medium hard to very hard, and are between slightly abrasive and 
abrasive. An SAB comminution circuit (SAG milling with pebble recycle and ball milling in closed circuit with 
hydrocyclones) was selected for the Nyanzaga processing plant to accommodate the spectrum of material 
hardness and competency observed from test work. Grind sensitivity test work indicates that Nyanzaga Gold 
Project ores are grind sensitive with gold extraction increasing with fineness of grind. Grind optimisation 
evaluations determined an optimum grind size P80 of 75 μm. 
Flowsheet definition and optimisation test work and techno -economic evaluations determined that 
Nyanzaga gold project ores are amenable to gravity recovery and cyanidation , and that a gravity 
recovery/cyanidation flowsheet achieves optimum results. 
Test work programs indicated that the gravity recovery stage added marginal benefit to the final gold 
extraction for most ore types. A gravity circuit has been included in the Nyanzaga process plant flowsheet to 
reduce reagent consumption in the CIL circuit;  to reduce the impact of coarse free gold on cyanidation 
performance and regulate plant feed grade; to allow for potentially improved leaching of gold associated 
with semi-refractory sulfide minerals that may report to the gravity concentrate stream; and to reduce the 
amount of coarse gold that may accumulate in gravity traps across the comminution circuit, which improves 
gold accountability and security outcomes. 
Gravity/cyanidation variability test work at optimised flowsheet conditions determined that average gold 
extractions by ore type ranged between 82.3% and 96.1%, and average silver extractions by ore type ranged 
between 26.5% and 66.1%. Gold leach kinetics were rapid, with most gold leaching occurring within four to 
eight hours. Silver leach kinetics were slower, with silver leaching being largely complete within 12 h, but 
continuing through to 24 h for some samples. 24 h leach time was selected for plant design. 
Tests on Nyanzaga deposit oxide, sandstone and chert ores, and Kilimani deposit oxide ores indicated that 
negligible preg-robbing or preg-borrowing occurs. Tests on Nyanzaga deposit mudstone ores identified preg-
borrowing characteristics, but it was noted that the activity of the carbon from CIL tests was sufficient to 
compete with the observed effects.  Head assays and mineralogical investigations suggest that the preg -
borrowing characteristics of the mudstone ore may be due to organic carbon, or fine-grained iron oxides or 
clay minerals (due to surface adsorption).

7 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
Pulp density optimisation tests  noted that gold extraction was unaffected by cyanidation slurry solids 
concentrations across the range tested, and 50% w/w solids concentration was selected for process plant 
design. Tests identified improved gold extraction occurred with a pre-oxidation stage before cyanidation, 
and elevated DO levels in cyanidation of 20 ppm through the addition of oxygen gas. Low to moderate rates 
of oxygen demand were observed, with higher gold grade samples showing a tendency to have slightly higher 
demands for oxygen. It is hypothesised that this observation is due to the association of gold with oxygen 
consuming sulfide minerals (pyrrhotite, arsenopyrite and pyrite) that are present in the Nyanzaga deposit 
fresh ores. A pre-oxidation step and elevated DO levels in cyanidation of 20  ppm through the addition of 
oxygen gas were selected for plant design. 
Low to moderate sodium cyanide and lime consumptions have been observed through test work. Estimated 
average plant CIL reagent additions have been estimated to range between 0.25 kg/t and 0.31 kg/t NaCN 
and 0.45 kg/t and 0.85 kg/t quicklime (90% w/w CaO) for oxide ores, and between 0.20 kg/t and 0.38 kg/t 
NaCN and 0.24 kg/t and 0.97 kg/t quicklime for fresh ores. 
It was noted that the Nyanzaga and Kilimani deposit ores contain elevated concentrations of mercury, arsenic 
and antimony. The process design includes a mercury handling circuit to mitigate the health hazards 
associated with mercury exposure. Test work and modelling indicates that soluble arsenic and soluble 
antimony will not have a significant effect on potential economic recovery of gold in CIL  and that soluble 
arsenic and soluble antimony will be contained within the tailings and process water systems. Provision has 
been made in sustaining capital for a water treatment plant should arsenic or antimony present operational 
challenges in the future. pH control is included in the process control design to mitigate gold passivation that 
can occur at high pH due to elevated antimony levels. 
Test work demonstrated that SO2/air cyanide detoxification can achieve residual CNWAD levels <50 mg/L at 
low stoichiometric ratios of SO2 to CNWAD, which aligns with industry guidelines for TSFs such as Standard of 
Practice 4.4 of International Cyanide Management Institute’s Mining Operations Verification Protocol (2021). 
SO2/air cyanide detoxification was selected for process plant design. 
Rheology test work highlighted that slurry streams containing solely Nyanzaga oxide ore and/or Kilimani 
deposit oxide ore should operate at a pulp density lower than 60% w/w solids to avoid viscosity related issues 
or be blended with fresh ores to operate at higher pulp densities. All ore types were demonstrated to be 
amenable to high-rate thickening with the selected flocculant, though Kilimani oxide ores only experienced 
minor carryover of solids to thickener overflow. The thickening and flocculant dosing parameters for Kilimani 
oxide ores indicated the highest duty and were therefore as the basis for sizing thickeners and the flocculant 
mixing plant. 
It is the opinion of the QP that metallurgical test work programs conducted are of sufficient scope and quality 
to support the proposed process plant design and production planning.

1.12 MINING METHODS 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project is proposed to be mined by open pit mining methods. Such mining methods are 
well established in Tanzania, and across other African operations owned and managed by Perseus Mining 
Limited. 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project (NGP) open pits will use a conventional hydraulic excavator and rigid off-highway 
rear dump truck fleet, with drill and blast where required in oxide, transitional and fresh rock material. Open 
pit mining will be undertaken with medium to large scale off-highway equipment, including 180 t – 350 t 
class excavators and 90 t – 150 t class dump trucks. 
Mining costs are based on contactor pricing supplied by Majesso Consulting and benchmarked against 
Perseus existing operations. The NGP open pit mining operation will have a proposed mining rate of 
approximately 50 Mt/a total material movement. Mining activities are proposed to be completed by a mining 
contractor, whose activities would include stripping free dig material such as topsoil, clays and highly 
weathered rock near surface.

Trucks will haul ore to surface ore stockpiles, with waste being hauled to, and disposed in, waste rock dumps. 
Stockpile rehandle will be by front-end loader. Mining bench heights are 10 m with 2.5 m flitches for selective 
mining to minimise ore loss and waste rock dilution. Bulk waste mining will also be completed on 10 m 
benches.

The pit design inter ramp slope angle varied depending on the degree of weathering of the material. A slope

included for the final 60 m of the pit, as required towards the end of pit life to maximise ore recovery and 
minimise waste mining. Rock is hauled to the surface, with ore placed on stockpiles at the ROM pad and 
waste dumped to waste rock dumps. 
1.13 RECOVERY METHODS 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project flowsheet will consist of the following unit processes: 
• Primary crushing with a single gyratory crusher to produce a coarse crushed product.

11 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
• A live stockpile from which ore is reclaimed to feed the milling circuit. 
• SAG milling with pebble recycle and ball milling in closed circuit with hydrocyclones (SAB comminution) 
to produce a grind size of 80% passing (P80) of 75 µm. 
• Gravity concentration and removal of coarse gold from the circulating load within the milling circuit, and 
treatment of gravity concentrate by intensive cyanidation and electrowinning. 
• Trash screening of the cyclone overflow stream, to remove wood and plastic trash or oversize material 
prior to cyanidation. 
• Pre-leach thickening of the trash screen underflow to increase the slurry density feeding the carbon-in-
leach (CIL) circuit and optimise water recycle within the process. 
• A pre-oxidation/CIL circuit to leach and adsorb gold and silver from the milled ore onto activated carbon. 
This circuit consists of one pre-oxidation tank, and six CIL tanks, providing a total of 24 hours leach and 
adsorption time. 
• A split AARL elution circuit for recovery of precious metals from loaded CIL carbon. 
• Electrowinning. 
• Carbon regeneration. 
• Smelting of electrowinning sludge, producing doré for sale 
• Mercury recovery from electrowinning sludge, and electrowinning cell , smelting furnace and carbon 
reactivation kiln off gases. 
• Thickening of CIL tailings to produce a higher solids concentration slurry for tailings storage facility (TSF) 
deposition and optimise water recycle within the process. 
• SO2/air detoxification of cyanide in tailings thickener underflow slurry. 
• Pumping of cyanide detoxification tailings to the TSF. 
• Return of TSF decant water for process use.

Power supply to Nyanzaga Gold Project will be sourced from the TANESCO national grid. The 220 kV supply

additional 220 kV feeder bay at the Bulyanhulu substation, approximately 53  km of 220  kV single circuit 
transmission line, and a substation at the Nyanzaga receiving end. The receiving end substation at Nyanzaga

will be installed consisting of a series of 2,000 kVA (standby rated) high speed diesel generators connected

A local microwave ground station will be installed at a site communications tower, to provide global satellite 
voice and data connection ; and a local telecommunications provider will be contracted to upgrade 
infrastructure to provide connection to the local, national and international telecommunications network. 
Internal communications and IT services will be via a site wide fibre optic network. A site-wide private mobile 
radio system will also be installed. 
Raw water will be drawn from the southwest tip of Smith Sound, the southern inlet of Lake Victoria, using a 
turret intake system (a floating water intake device on the end of a hose that avoids drawing in sediment or 
floating material) and will be delivered by two self-priming pump sets to a 13.5 km delivery pipeline to the 
Project site. The pipeline will be buried outside of the SML to reduce the risk of unauthorised water use. The 
pipeline located inside the SML will not be buried. 
The TSF will be located south of the open pit and will be constructed as a single cell storage facility consisting 
of a multi -zoned earthfill downstream constructed embankment designed to store the LOM processing 
production profile of tailings. The total footprint area (including the basin area) will be approximately 130 ha 
for Stage 1 of the TSF, increasing to approximately 225 ha for the final stage of the TSF. The facility will be 
constructed as a paddock type storage facility utilising natural ridges to reduce the volume of embankment 
fill, and the waste dump to buttress the northern embankment. The TSF will be raised annually using the 
downstream method of construction. 
Tailings will be discharged into the TSF by sub-aerial deposition methods, using multiple spigots at regular 
intervals along the southern perimeter. Tailings will be deposited following the deposition plan, developed 
to locate the supernatant pond towards the decant area in the northern part of the facility and away from 
the embankments. Supernatant water will be removed from the TSF by a decant pumping system with a 
turret intake and returned to the process plant. 
Preliminary design of surface water and sediment control facilities has been completed and includes separate 
diversion channels and sediment control dams to handle runoff depending on the area that the water 
collection has occurred and the contained level of sediment and other contamination. The design of these 
facilities will be finalised in parallel with the broader site infrastructure design.

Gold is a commodity freely traded on the world market for which there is a steady demand from numerous

international markets or delivered into forward sales contracts. The refiner wil l invoice Perseus for costs

1.16 ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES, PERMITTING AND SOCIAL OR COMMUNITY 
IMPACT 
An Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) was undertaken and submitted to the National 
Environment Management Council (NEMC) for approval in late 2017. The ESIA comprises several 
management plans which describe how project activities might impact on the natural environment in which 
it occurs and set out clear commitments from the company taking the action on how those impacts will be 
avoided, minimised and managed. 
Since 2018, additional studies and engineering works have been undertaken on the Project. As a result of 
changes in the Site layout, SMCL submitted an updated Environmental and Social Management Plan to NEMC 
in July 2023. Another update will be prepared by Perseus and resubmitted to the NEMC with the changes to 
production scale and site layout related to this Study that have been finalised in 2024. 
A conceptual mine closure plan (MCP) was prepared and submitted as part of the ESIA. A detail MCP will be 
submitted to the Ministry of Minerals for approval within one year of commencing operations and 
subsequently updated at least every three years. 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project will cause both physical and economic displacement in the villages of Sotta and 
Nyabila. A Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) is being implemented to support those affected. The RAP aims to 
ensure affected people are compensated fairly and supported to restore or improve their livelihoods and 
living standards, and follows Tanzanian law (Land Act 1999, Mining Act 2017) and international standards 
(IFC Performance Standard 5) to ensure fair and transparent resettlement and compensation. All affected 
households, whether physically or economically displaced, can participate in a livelihood restoration program 
tailored to their level of impact. 
Surveys and studies to support the RAP were completed in February 2023. The Project has since advanced 
the RAP with compensation payments completed for over 93% of the project affected persons. A housing 
relocation construction program is underway, and the scheduling of house builds will be sequenced to ensure 
that areas of the SML are available to achieve Project development scope and schedule. 
Although a number of environmental and social impacts have been identified, it is expected that these will 
be successfully abated through implementation of a range of mitigations and management measures. At the 
same time there will be many positive impacts  expected, including improved housing, community 
infrastructure, community contributions to improve services, livelihood developments and employment 
opportunities for local community members.

1.19 INTERPRETATION AND CONCLUSIONS 
This Report summarises the results of an updated Feasibility Study for the Nyanzaga Gold Project, which 
demonstrates the technical and economic viability of a large open pit mining operation on the Nyanzaga and 
Kilimani orebodies.  
Data that inform the resource estimate are considered to be representative and free of any biases or other 
factors that may materially impact the reliability of the sampling or significantly affect confidence in 
estimated resources. Checks to confirm the validity of the drilling database indicate that it forms a sufficiently 
reliable basis for resource estimation. Drilling activities are ongoing at the Nyanzaga Gold Project with a focus 
on infill and depth extensions at the Nyanzaga and Kilimani deposits, as well as early-stage exploration on 
granted tenure. 
Perseus has performed an economic analysis related to the Nyanzaga Gold Project to Feasibility Study level 
of accuracy at the forecasted metal prices, production rates, metal recoveries, and capital and operating 
costs estimated in this Report. Perseus confirms that the positive economic outcome supports the Mineral 
Reserve estimate. 
The QP is of the opinion that Mineral Reserves were estimated using industry -accepted practices and 
conform to the CIM Definition Standards and the JORC Code. Mineral Reserves stated in this report are based 
on open pit mining methods. The Mineral Reserves are acceptable to support mine planning. 
Open pit mining of the Nyanzaga Gold Project is considered reasonable and technically viable based on the 
parameters and assumptions contained within this report and based on Perseus’ extensive open pit mining 
experience in other African jurisdictions. 
The results of comminution and metallurgical test work conducted across the Nyanzaga and Kilimani deposits 
are considered by the QP to be of sufficient scope and quality to support the proposed process plant design 
and production planning. The single stage crushing and SAB comminution circuit selected can accommodate

the spectrum of material hardness and competency observed from test work, and can achieve the target 
plant throughput and grind size. It has been demonstrated that the Nyanzaga and Kilimani deposits are ‘free-
milling’ and amenable to gold recovery by a standard gravity and CIL flowsheet.  
Infrastructure for the process plant, and the Project more widely, has been considered and defined to 
Feasibility Study level. Key enabling infrastructure for the Project includes the Ngoma bypass road, 220 kV 
connection to the TANESCO grid, external communications, water abstraction system from Lake Victoria, 
TSF, MSA, permanent accommodation camp, and other operational buildings. 
Environmental permitting for the Nyanzaga Gold Project mine is up to date, and Perseus has a positive and 
constructive relationship with the government, and with other stakeholders and the local community. 
Ongoing application and renewal of licenses and agreements with the Government of Tanzania and other 
stakeholders, including local communities, is well managed and understood, and there are not expected to 
be any delays or impediments to project development or operation. 
1.20 RECOMMENDATIONS 
Based upon the Nyanzaga Gold Project Feasibility Study, the following key recommendations are identified: 
• Pursue the current planned drilling programs within the Nyanzaga area, which aim to add to reported 
Mineral Resources. The work program will involve additional drilling as both infill and at depth for each 
of Nyanzaga and Kilimani. 
• Complete additional geotechnical drilling, test work and analysis to improve confidence and precision of 
pit and waste dump geotechnical parameters. 
• Complete metallurgical test work and analysis to further improve understanding of ore variability and 
improve confidence and precision of operating and cost parameters used for ongoing business planning 
processes. 
• Once the additional drilling, geotechnical work, and metallurgical test work referred to above has been 
completed, Mineral Reserves should be updated based on any additions to Mineral Resources and any 
changes to geotechnical and ore processing parameters, and the results of such work should be publicly 
released. 
• The contractor mining tender process for the Nyanzaga Gold Project should continue in order to test the 
market for real-world mining costs and enable mobilisation of a suitable open pit mining contractor in 
time for the pre-strip of the Nyanzaga Gold Project. 
• Increase knowledge regarding PAF waste distribution, and develop detailed plans for waste dump design 
that includes encapsulation. 
• Proceed with detailed design of the mineral processing plant and Project enabling infrastructure. 
• Complete a study considering a full -capacity power station located adjacent to the Project 220  kV 
switchyard. Renewable generation options are to be considered. 
• Applications for Permits required for the Project should be made in a timely manner in order to support 
the development and execution of the Nyanzaga Gold Project. 
• Due to changes between the previous OreCorp DFS and the layouts proposed in this Study by Perseus, 
an updated Environmental and Social Management Plan will be required for resubmission to the NEMC. 
Perseus to complete necessary updates and studies required to update the ESMP.  
• Progress updates to the closure cost estimate to reflect the most recent level of understanding of the 
Project. 
• Conduct further studies on the Project hydrogeology, including updating models with the latest structural 
interpretation of the open pit, conducting pit void water balance modelling, and modelling of the pit lake 
water quality at mine closure.

4. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION AND LOCATION  
4.1 LOCATION 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project (the Project) is located in north-western Tanzania, south of Lake Victoria within 
the Sengerema District of the Mwanza Region. The Project is approximately 60 km southwest of Mwanza 
(Tanzania’s second largest city) and 7  km southeast of Ngoma, with the total area of the Project being 
16,085 ha. The Project is approximately 60 km east of the Geita Gold Mine and 35  km northeast of the 
Bulyanhulu Gold Mine, at 2°58’S Latitude and 32°42’E Longitude as shown in Figure 4-1.

4.4 MINERAL RIGHTS AND LEGAL OBLIGATIONS 
4.4.1 MINING ACT 
The Mining Act, CAP.  123 is the principal legislation that governs mining activities and mineral rights. 
According to the Act the entire property and control over minerals in Tanzania is vested in the President in 
trust for the People of Tanzania. The Government shall have lien over any material, substance, product or 
associated products extracted from the mining operations or mineral processing. 
In practice the Mining Commission has overall responsibility for minerals including advising the Government 
on minerals matters, reviewing mining sector activities and promoting development. The Mining Commission 
also serves as a conduit between the Government and prospective investors. 
The main laws governing mining operations in Tanzania are the following: 
• Mining Act, 2010. 
• The Natural Wealth and Resources (Permanent Sovereignty) Act, 2017 (Sovereignty Act). 
• The Natural Wealth and Resources Contracts (Review and Renegotiation of Unconscionable Terms) Act, 
2017 (Unconscionable Terms Act). 
• The Occupational Safety and Health Act, CAP. 424. 
• The Mining (Mineral Rights) Regulations, 2018. 
• The Mining (Local Content) Regulations, 2018. 
• The Mining (State Participation) Regulations, 2022. 
• The Mining (Government Minerals Warehouse) Regulations, 2021. 
• Mining (Mineral Beneficiation) Regulation, 2018. 
• Corporate Social Responsibility Regulations, 2023. 
4.4.2 TENURE 
The SML shall remain valid for the period of the life of the ore body indicated in the Feasibility Study provided 
in support of the application, or such period as the applicant may request (in the case of SML 653/2021 this 
is 15 years) unless it is sooner cancelled, suspended or surrendered in accordance with the law. 
The SML shall cease to subsist if the holder of the licence ceases mining operations or abandons the area 
where mining operations are undertaken without prior permission of the Mining Commission.

42

Renewal of the SML shall be subject to conditions stipulated under Section 45 of The Mining Act. 
4.4.3 MINE DEVELOPMENT AND PRODUCTION 
Before commencement of mining operations, the holder of the SML shall ensure the proposed plan for 
relocation, resettlement and payment of compensation to people within the area where mining operations 
will be undertaken is implemented in accordance with the provisions of The Land Act, or the Village Land Act, 
as the case may be. 
Before carrying out any work or activity within the area where mining operations will be undertaken, the 
holder of the SML, contractor or subcontractor shall set up a project office within the area of land in the 
District where the mining project is located. 
The holder of the SML, contractor or subcontractor shall commence mining activities within eighteen 
calendar months from the date of grant of the SML or such further period as may be determined by the 
Mining Commission on the basis of plans, general designs for the mine and related facilities as well as other 
ancillary operations. SMCL has met this requirement. 
4.4.4 METHOD OF OPERATIONS 
The holder of the SML shall carry out the program of mining operations in accordance with the program of 
mining operations approved by the Mining Commission, as may be amended, and satisfy obligations under 
the SML, and take full responsibility and assume attendant risks. 
The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor shall take all reasonable measures necessary to secure the 
safety, health and welfare of persons engaged in the mining operations in or about the area to which the 
SML apply and ensure safety or properties in accordance with the governing laws. 
The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor shall, in respect of the mine, take all measures necessary 
to avert occurrence of accidents whether accidental or premeditated and to observe and satisfy conditions 
stipulated under The Occupational Safety and Health Act. 
4.4.5 BENEFICIATION 
Unless agreed otherwise with the Government, the holder of a SML shall set at least 20% of gold produced 
aside for beneficiation and trading in Tanzania. The Government and SMCL have agreed that any such in-
country beneficiation shall be at a London Bullion Market Association (LBMA) accredited refinery. 
4.4.6 ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT 
The holder of a SML and any other person who exercises powers or performs functions or carries duties in 
relation therewith shall be under statutory obligation to comply with the Environmental Management Plan 
approved by NEMC as well as environmental principles and safeguards prescribed under the Environmental 
Management Act, CAP. 191, and other relevant laws. 
The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor shall ensure that management of production, 
transportation, storage, treatment and disposal of waste arising out of mining operations is carried out in 
accordance with environmental principles and safeguards prescribed by the Environmental Management 
Act. 
The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor may, for the purpose of the paragraph above contract a 
separate competent entity to manage transportation, storage, treatment or disposal of waste arising out of 
mining operations. 
The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor shall ensure that regular environmental audits, monitoring 
and evaluation are carried out to avert environmental spoil, degradation and hazardous substances which 
are or may be harmful to human beings, and or the environment.

The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor shall develop and adopt Mine Closure and Rehabilitation 
Plans of the area where mining operations are carried out. 
4.4.7 LOCAL CONTENT 
The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor, carrying out mining activities, shall ensure that a Local 
Content Plan is developed and implemented in accordance with the requirements of Part VIII of The Mining 
Act, CAP. 123 as further detailed under the Mining (Local Content) Regulations, 2018 and the Mining 
Commission (Guidelines for Submission of Local Content Plan), 2018. 
For the purposes of the paragraph above, the holder of a SML, contractor, subcontractor and other allied 
entity are required to make a declaration of adherence to local content requirements in the form set out in 
the Mining Commission (Guidelines for Submission of Local Content Plan), 2018. 
The holder of a SML, contractor or subcontractor shall submit any proposed local content plans to the Mining 
Commission substantially in the form set out in the Mining Commission (Guidelines for Submission of Local 
Content Plan) 2018 and in accordance with the Corporate Social Responsibility Regulations, 2023. 
4.4.8 CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY 
The holder of a SML shall, on an annual basis, prepare a credible Social Responsibility Plan jointly agreed by 
the relevant local government authority or local government authorities upon consultation with the Minister 
responsible for local government and the Minister responsible for finance. 
The holder of a SML shall ensure that the Corporate Social Responsibility Plan prepared is congruent and 
responsive to guidelines for corporate social responsibility developed by the relevant local government 
authority in terms of section 105(4) of The Mining Act, CAP. 123 and make a declaration specified under the 
Schedule to the Mining Commission (Guidelines for Submission of Local Content Plan), 2018. 
4.4.9 INTEGRITY PLEDGE 
The holder of a SML shall undertake to comply with the Statement of Integrity Pledge in accordance with 
Part VIII of The Mining Act and The Mining (Integrity Pledge) Regulations, 2018. 
The Statement of Integrity Pledge referred to above shall be in the form specified under The Mining (Integrity 
Pledge) Regulations, 2018.

5.1 ACCESSIBILITY 
Many international airlines fly into Tanzania from Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere in Africa. Regular 
commercial domestic flights, supplemented by charter airlines, provide connections to Mwanza Airport. 
The Project will rely on import of major equipment and specialist materials and consumables through the 
Port of Dar es Salaam. 
Road access between Dar es Salaam and Mwanza is just over 1,100  km, with access to the Project from  
Mwanza by the sealed Mwanza – Geita Highway, crossing Smith Sound (an arm of Lake Victoria) via ferry or 
the recently constructed Kigongo – Busisi Bridge (John Pombe Magufuli Bridge), and then travelling on the 
unsealed regional road network for 35 km from Sengerema to Ngoma. The Project area is approximately 
9 km southeast of Ngoma, and an unsealed road is currently under construction to bypass Ngoma township 
and reach the Nyanzaga site. This road construction is key enabling infrastructure for Project delivery and 
operations. 
The national road network is generally well maintained by the Tanzania National Roads Agency (TANROADS) 
as far as Ngoma. Rural roads are managed by TARURA. Construction of the Ngoma bypass road is being

Key elements of Project transportation and logistics are discussed further in Section 18.1. 
5.2 PHYSIOGRAPHY 
The central part of the Project is dominated by ranges of hills which run roughly northwest–southeast (Figure 
5-1). Site topography ranges from a height of approximately 1,130 m above sea level (at the lowest valley 
point) to 1,473 m above sea level (Nyanzaga hill) (Sotta Mining Corporation Limited, 2023). The process plant 
will be constructed at approximately 1,210 m above sea level (Lycopodium, 2024a). The hilly ground is 
covered by light to medium miombo woodland, surrounded by gently sloping ground, proximal to the hills 
often covered by indurated laterite, rock boulders and gravels. 
Most of the areas to the south and to the east towards Lake Victoria are relatively flat-lying and are covered 
by old lake sediments of black cotton soil (mbuga), parts of which are waterlogged during the rainy season 
and are mainly used as farmland. There are few seasonal rivers, the main one being the Wingi River which 
drains water from the Project area to Lake Victoria.

5.3 CLIMATE 
The climate of Tanzania ranges from tropical along the coast, to temperate in the highlands, due mainly to 
the widely varying topography of the country. The central, northern and western regions (e.g., Mwanza, 
Kagera, Kigoma, Shinyanga and Tabora), including the area in which the Project is located, have a climate 
moderated by the highland plateau. The Nyanzaga Gold Project is located in an area that has a Köppen 
climate classification of tropical savannah climate (Aw) (Knight Piésold, 2021a). 
Weather data from both the Mwanza Meteorological Station (MMS) , operated by the Tanzania 
Meteorological Agency (TMA), and a weather station located at the Nyanzaga site have been used as primary 
data sources to understand the climate of the Nyanzaga Gold Project. 
Monthly precipitation data, from the site weather station from the periods of 2012 to 2020 and 2022 to 
2024, and the  MMS, indicate that the mean monthly rainfall over the period varied between 0 mm and 
254 mm (Lycopodium, 2024a), (Knight Piésold, 2021a). The mean annual total precipitation is estimated to 
be between 928 mm and 1,063 mm, with approximately 110 wet days per year (Lycopodium, 2024a), (Knight 
Piésold, 2021a). The 100-year average recurrence interval (ARI) wet scenario precipitation is estimated to be 
1,698 mm, and the 100-year ARI dry scenario precipitation is estimated to be 623 mm (Knight Piésold, 
2021a). 
The rainfall pattern suggests a bimodal rainy season comprised of the long rains of Masika between March 
and May and short rains of Vuli between October and December (which is typical for the Lake Victoria basin). 
The dry season occurs between June and September, when the average monthly rainfall is between 0 mm 
and 38 mm per month (Lycopodium, 2024a). Relative humidity measured at the Nyanzaga site ranges from 
14.9% during the dry season to 99.8% during the rainy seasons (Lycopodium, 2024a). Annual pan evaporation 
is estimated to be 2,378  mm, and annual lake evaporation is estimated to be 1, 685 mm (Knight Piésold, 
2021a). 
Temperature records, from the site weather station from the periods of 2012 to 2020 and 2022 to 2024, and 
the MMS, indicate that the mean monthly maximum temperature varies between 25°C and 34°C, and the 
mean monthly minimum temperature varied between 15°C and 23°C (Lycopodium, 2024a). The highest 
temperature recorded was 41.7°C and the lowest temperature recorded was 14.5°C (Lycopodium, 2024a).

Workforce planning efforts have commenced for Nyanzaga and represent a key component in establishing a

5.7 LOCAL ECONOMY 
Agriculture is the main economic activity of the people in the local area. Igalula Ward has arable land of 
approximately 22.7 km2 that supports production of various crops throughout the year. There are two main 
agricultural seasons determined by rainfall patterns, which include short rains between October and 
December, and long (heavy) rains that occur in March to May. 
The primary source of livelihood for most households is subsistence farming , with approximately 12% 
depending on other sources including artisanal mining, fishing, salaried employment, general labour, 
livestock keeping and small trading. For most subsistence farmers, crop sales are their main source of income. 
Other supplementary sources of income are sale of livestock, firewood, charcoal, medicinal plants, processed 
food products, and grass/reeds. 
Approximately 7.7 km2 (33%) of the total SML area is uncultivated, being the hilly areas of Kilimani Ridge, 
Nyanzaga Hill and Nyamtukuza Hill. Most of the remaining land is used for food and cash crops. The main 
food and cash crops grown are maize and rice, and to a lesser ext ent crops such as lentils, beans, ground 
nuts, sweet potatoes, cassava, chickpeas , and sorghum. Cash crops include cotton, sisal , and aloe vera. 
Mango trees are the main fruit tree in the area. Most households have a land size of 1 to 10 acres.

7. GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND MINERALISATION  
7.1 REGIONAL GEOLOGY 
The Nyanzaga Project is located on the north-eastern flank of the Sukumaland Greenstone Belt, representing 
one of the six greenstone belts within the Tanzanian portion of the Lake Victoria Goldfield. The greenstone 
belts contain a diverse sequence of volcanic and sedimentary rocks of mostly greenschist metamorphic 
grade, which host numerous gold prospects and active mines (e.g. Bulyanhulu, Geita, and North Mara). The 
greenstone sequences within these belts have been divided into the Nyanzian Supergroup (Nyanzian) and 
Kavirondian Supergroup (Kavirondian) (Stockley, 1943; Borg & Krogh, 1977). 
Further division of the Nyanzian has been proposed into a “Lower Series” of mafic -intermediate volcanic 
(minor ultramafic) with subordinate iron formations and clastic sediments, and an “Upper Series” of felsic to 
intermediate volcanics, volcaniclastics, iron formations, chert, mudstone, and sandstones. The Kavirondian, 
which unconformably overlies the Nyanzian, is dominated by coarse clastic sediments (sandstones and 
conglomerates) (Figure 7-1).

7.2 LOCAL GEOLOGY 
The Project is situated on the north -eastern flank of the Sukumaland Greenstone Belt. Rock sequences 
comprise Nyanzian-aged sequences of mafic volcanics in the far south -west and banded -iron-formation, 
tuffs, mudstone, sandstone and epiclastics of general volcanogenic origin and massive sulfide lenses and 
volcanics of rhyodacitic to andesitic composition. The sequences are tightly folded and strike generally west-
northwest. 
Historical petrology work indicated the protolith types at Nyanzaga included volcanic arenite and tuffs; 
siliceous and ferruginous chemical sediments and reworked tuffs; pelite (mudstone, silty mudstone), calc-
arenite with primary carbonate matrix; and volcanogenic clastic sediments including andesitic crystal-lithic 
tuff, polymictic breccia and layered greywacke (Mason, 2011). The country rock suites at Nyanzaga show a 
dacitic to andesitic volcanogenic composition (Henkel, 2012). 
In the central part of the project, the Nyanzaga and Kilimani groups are defined. The Nyanzaga Group is 
divided into a sequence of three broad mappable units from drill core and outcrop mapping and are in 
stratigraphical order as follows:  
1. Nyanzaga Upper Volcaniclastic Formation.  
2. Nyanzaga Central Formation (formerly Mine Formation). 
3. Nyanzaga Lower Volcaniclastic Formation. 
These three units are folded into the north-northwest plunging Nyanzaga Anticline. These sequences are in 
turn overlain by the Kilimani Group which appears to be tectonically dislocated from the underlying Nyanzaga 
Group by faulting and potential earlier thrusts. A map displaying the interpreted geology of the Nyanzaga 
area is presented in Figure 7-2.

7.3 STRUCTURE 
7.3.1 REGIONAL 
Distinctive structural domains are evident in the regional aeromagnetics and are highlighted in Figure 7-6. 
These domains preserve distinct structural characteristics, and there is a particularly large contrast between 
intensely deformed domains and relative flat-signature low-intensity deformed domains. These structural 
boundaries are also likely to locate changes in metamorphic grade between different domains with different 
structural and metamorphic histories.  
The Nyanzaga domain has a unique signature in terms of folds and magnetic units, and may represent a 
distinct sub-basin with fault bound compartments. This working interpretation is based on the evidence of 
local facies and thickness variations (which are observed in the field and in drill core) and the presence of 
massive sulfides which are likely fault controlled. The basin -bounding extensional faults are likely later 
reactivated in inversion during compression and are an important aspect of the local scale architecture of 
the Nyanzaga domain.

7.3.2 LOCAL 
A series of different faulting sets has been recognised across the Nyanzaga project area . These include 
observed outcrop positions with suggested sinistral movement; others with inferred dextral movement; a 
series of steep faults sub-parallel to bedding; and a number of low angle thrust faults. Additionally, east-west 
trending normal faults with minor displacement have been identified. 
The interaction of these various fault orientations results in the definition of numerous fault block domains.

proximal ankerite - sericite dominated and quartz-pyrite alteration. Three key alteration assemblages have 
been identified. These include:

increased arsenopyrite concentration. 
The Far East Fault mineralisation is defined by strong alteration, which is zoned from proximal silica-sericite 
to more distal carbonate alteration. En -echelon arrays of sub -vertical quartz veins occur immediately 
adjacent to the silica-core and indicate a sinistral sense of movement of the Far East Fault zone. 
The presence of molybdenite, scheelite, tourmaline and the massive carbonate influx into the alteration 
system supports the potential of an intrusive body in proximity to Nyanzaga. 
The current interpretation indicates that there is a distinct lithological control and most the gold appears to 
be hosted by iron rich sediments in the form of an extensive stock -work of carbonate, quartz veins, and 
quartz-carbonate breccias. Preferential grade enhancement occurs in selected altered units such as the thick 
cherts, silica-dolomite altered medium grained sandstones, brecciated silica-carbonate altered mudstones; 
or in the late quartz veins as free gold. High-gold grades occur in narrow 5 to 20 mm wide tensional quartz 
veins that developed as conjugate sets and dip moderately to the southwest and southeast. Evidence 
suggests these veins may have developed along the axis of plunging parasitic folds in the area of the cherts; 
or with an apparent pr eference for developing in dolomitised and silicified, medium to coarse grained 
sandstone host rocks.

8. DEPOSIT TYPES  
The Lake Victoria Gold Field hosts numerous small-scale and several large-scale orogenic gold deposits. The 
orogenic deposits are found in regionally metamorphosed terrains of volcanic or sedimentary rocks, of all 
ages from the mid Archaean to the Tertiary. At the broadest scale the deposits were formed during 
compressional or transpressional deformation processes at convergent plate margins in accretionary and 
collisional orogenic events, which are typified by the emplacement of abundant granitoid plutons and 
batholiths. In both tectonic regimes, hydrated marine sedimentary sequences  are added to continental 
margins. Subduction related thermal events then drive extensive hydrothermal fluid systems resulting in the 
emplacement of gold bearing quartz veins from depths of 15 km-20 km to surface. See Figure 8-1 for tectonic 
setting. 
 
 
Figure 8-1: Tectonic settings of gold-rich epigenetic mineral deposits. Vertical scale is exaggerated to allow schematic depths 
of formation of various deposit styles to be shown. Adapted from Groves et al (1998). Abbreviations: VHMS = volcanic hosted 
massive sulfide. 
 
Mineralisation takes place post the deformation of the host rock but is syn -orogenic with respect to the 
ongoing deep crustal, subduction related thermal processes. Fluid flow is probably driven by episodes of 
major pressure fluctuations during seismic events. The majority of orogenic gold deposits in metamorphic 
terranes are located adjacent to first-order, deep-crustal fault zones, which may extend along strike for tens 
to hundreds of kilometres with widths of as much as a few thousand meters. 
Mineralisation formed as vein fill of second- and third-order shears and faults, particularly at jogs or changes 
in strike along the crustal fault zones. Mineralisation styles vary from stockworks and breccias in shallow, 
brittle regimes, through laminated crack-seal veins and sigmoidal vein arrays in brittle-ductile crustal regions, 
to replacement- and disseminated-type ore bodies in deeper, ductile environments (i .e., a continuum 
model). 
Orogenic deposits may be subdivided into epizonal (<6 km), mesozonal (6-12 km), and hypozonal (>12 km) 
subtypes based on pressure -temperature conditions of ore formation  (Groves, Goldfarb, Gebre-Mariam, 
Hagemann, & Robert, 1998). Most orogenic gold deposits contain 2 to 5 percent sulfide minerals and have 
gold/silver ratios from 5 to 10 and gold fineness >900. Pyrite and arsenopyrite are the dominant sulfide 
minerals, whereas pyrrhotite is more important in higher temperature ores and base metals are not highly 
anomalous. Alteration intensity, width, and assemblage vary with the host rock, but carbonates, sulfides, 
muscovite, chlorite, K-feldspar, biotite, tourmaline, and albite are generally present, Ore fluids were, in most

69 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
cases, near-neutral pH, slightly reduced, dominated by sulfide complexes and CO2 rich, with low to moderate 
salinities. 
The Nyanzaga mineralisation is a member of the orogenic clan of gold deposits. It is hosted by a sequence of 
chemical and clastic sediments (chert/sandstone/siltstone), and it displays the typical alteration features of 
an orogenic deposit, such as pervasive carbonate alteration, going from distal ferroan calcite dominated to 
proximal ankerite and sericite dominated and quartz-pyrite alteration. There is a distinct lithological control; 
the majority of the gold is hosted by Fe -rich sediments in form of an extensive stock work (crustiform 
carbonate veins, quartz veins, quartz carbonate breccias). The brittle deformation style allows the 
mineralisation to be classified as epizonal.

10.1.2 COLLAR SURVEYS 
A Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS) survey work program was undertaken to survey accurately 
any preserved historical drill collars; validate existing historical 2012 control and survey pickups; and in 
addition, the centre lines of all tracks and benches were also surveyed. 
The work was carried out by professional surveyors, Nile Surveys (Uganda) Ltd in March 2017 and was 
completed in two phases on and around the Nyanzaga Hill. This work found that: 
• Historical Acacia holes were very accurate (<10 cm difference) in nothing and easting, with elevations 
generally ±1-2 m, while several were in the ±4–6 m range, due to elevations being derived from a 
historical 2011 DTM surface. 
• The mine datum pillars (located in the exploration camp compound) established by Acacia using Ramani 
Surveys were very accurate for the mine grid purpose, but due to the Arc 1960 transform used, a shift of 
about 2.5 m southeast with respect to government topography and cadastral maps occurred. 
The DGPS collar survey information was updated into the database, with the latest DGPS data superseding 
previous collar coordinates. The database was configured to store different generations of survey data, 
maintaining all historical records. 
10.1.3 DOWNHOLE SURVEYS 
A combination of poor ground conditions, weathering characteristics and in some instances driller practices 
(i.e., removal of the stabiliser rod in coincident clay and high waterflow areas to reduce chances of bogging) 
have influenced the down-hole trajectories in certain areas of the project. 
Subsequent review of historical down-hole survey data showed similar tendencies to deviate at Nyanzaga. 
Gyroscopic re-surveys of several holes with excessive azimuth deviations were undertaken and confirmed 
localised, significant deflections (even with stabiliser rods fitted) in the unstable portions of the oxide zone. 
Once into fresh rock hole deviation was minimal. 
Deviation caused by strongly magnetic mudstones and pyrrhotite has also been an observed issue in older 
surveys undertaken with a downhole survey probe based on magnetic readings. Gyroscopic tool readings in 
these strata produce a more reliable hole trace, and as such have superseded the magnetic down-hole survey 
probe data where undertaken and have been updated in the database.

10.1.5 RC SAMPLING  
10.1.5.1 SUB SAHARA RESOURCES 
Samples were collected at 1  m intervals in plastic bags and their weight (25  – 35 kg) was recorded in a 
logbook. Wet samples were collected in polythene bags and allowed to air dry before splitting. Prior to 
September 2005, the samples were combined into 3 m composites by taking a 300 g scoop from 10 –15 kg 
1 m interval, then mixing it with 300 g scoops from each of two adjacent samples. The 1 kg composite sample 
was then submitted to SGS Mwanza laboratory (SGS) for preparation and analysis. Magnetic susceptibility 
readings were taken every metre.  
The individual 1  m samples were stored for future assaying in case of positive results obtained by 3  m 
composite. After September 2005, 1  m split samples of 1  kg weight were submitted directly to SGS for 
analysis and the remaining weight approximately 15  – 20 kg was stored on site. Samples were placed in 
plastic bags, labelled and stacked in order on plastic sheets. Samples were catalogued in a register so that 
samples could readily be retrieved, and sample stacks were covered with plastics and secured.  
10.1.5.2 BARRICK EXPLORATION AFRICA/ACACIA 
All RC drillholes were sampled at 1 m intervals for the entire length of the hole, where possible. Each sample 
was collected into a plastic bucket large enough to hold approximately 40  kg of cuttings, which was held 
below the cyclone spigot by a drill helper. To avoid sample contamination after a drill run was completed, 
blow-backs were carried out at the end of each of the 6 m runs by the driller whereby the percussion bit was 
lifted off the bottom of the hole and the hole blown clean. If water was encountered in the hole, the driller 
was directed to dry out the hole by increasing air pressure into the hole and lifting and lowering the rods 
prior to continuing the drilling. The sample cuttings for each metre were weighed using a spring scale and 
recorded.  
Following weighing, the sample contents from the bucket were disgorged into a Gilson riffle splitter. A sample 
was collected on one side of the splitter as a reject. The material collected in the residue buckets on the other 
side of the splitter was poured back into the splitter and a 4 – 5 kg sample was collected from the second 
split in a small pre-labelled and tagged plastic bag for dispatch to the assay laboratory. The bag was then 
folded over several times and stapled to prevent sample leakage. The contents of the second bucket were 
poured into a pre-labelled plastic sample bag, containing the sample interval marked on an aluminium or 
plastic tag, for storage at the Nyanzaga camp.  
The splitter and sample collection boxes were cleaned by tapping the box/splitter with rubber mallet or stick 
after every metre drilled. A record was made at the drill site of the sample identity numbers and 
corresponding intervals, and cross checked against the pre-drilling sample sheet.  
Remaining drill cuttings for each metre were placed on the ground, in drill order as piles in rows of ten 
samples for logging. Representative sieved/washed samples were also taken from each metre drilled. These 
samples and chips were then put in numerical order into a chip box. Drill cuttings of the representative rock 
types and geological interest intersected in the hole were also archived in chip trays.  
10.1.5.3 INDAGO 
The bulk samples for every 1 m interval were collected via a cyclone into a plastic bucket which was then 
weighed prior to sampling using a triple-tier riffle splitter. Care was taken to ensure the splitter and plastic 
buckets were cleaned between each sample, and the cyclone cleaned at the end of each rod. As the 12.5%
