10.1.6 DIAMOND CORE SAMPLING AND CORE RECOVERIES 
10.1.6.1 SUB SAHARA RESOURCES 
The core was correctly fitted in the core boxes prior to sampling to ensure that only one side of the core was 
sampled consistently. The core was then split using a diamond saw and sampled and QAQC samples inserted 
accordingly. Sample length varied between 0.5 m and 1.0 m and only half of the cut core was sent to the 
laboratory, the other half was marked with a sample number tag and stored in racks at Nyanzaga site. Prior 
to storing the core, Apparent Relative Density (ARD) measurements were taken (every metre) and the data 
incorporated into the database. The gold assay values received were written in red permanent ink on the 
corresponding core intervals.  
10.1.6.2 BARRICK EXPLORATION AFRICA/ACACIA 
A geologist marked the sample intervals and cutting line, which was then placed on the core with a 1  cm 
offset from the orientation line: the remaining half of the core contains the orientation line. The technicians 
split the core using an electric core saw in two equal halves which are placed side by side back into the core 
box. The same half of core was always sampled. Where there is no orientation, a line is chosen to at 90° to 
the predominant structure so that each cut half of the core will be a mirror image.  
Core cutting by diamond saw was conducted in a dedicated core saw shed, while unconsolidated material 
was split using spoons or trowels. Core was cut in half, or in the case of unconsolidated material, half the 
material scooped out on one side of the tray. A 1 m half core was removed from the core box for assaying. 
Each sample interval was placed in a plastic bag with a sample ticket. The bag was labelled with the hole and 
sample numbers using a marker pen.  
After communicating with the responsible geologist, the core was sampled by a trained technician in intervals 
up to 1 m and no less than 0.25 m. In general, the core was sampled at 1 m intervals, however, in some cases, 
such as ore zones, samples were taken at irregular intervals to honour the nature of the lithology and 
mineralisation. The sample number was placed on the remaining half of core, as well as written on the core 
with permanent marker. The remaining sample number tickets were placed in the core box. The samples 
were placed in plastic bags and then placed in a bucket with a security seal and put in a secure area until 
collected and transported to the laboratory.  
10.1.6.3 INDAGO 
The diamond core was cut using a simple brick saw into equal halves; one half of the core was collected for 
each 1 m interval (or where the supervising geologist specified) into a calico bag making sure that the same 
half was consistently sampled down the hole and that any core orientations present were preserved in the 
remaining core. No sample interval was less than 20 cm or exceeded 1.5 m.

It was audited by Smee and Associates Consulting Ltd in 2008. 
Additional assaying was completed at ALS which has received SANAS accreditation against ISO/IEC 
17025:2017 for gold assaying with the accreditation number T0470. 
Both SGS and ALS are commercial laboratories that are independent to Perseus. 
Both laboratories employed similar sample preparation procedures. The entire sample was emptied into a 
stainless steel drying tray and dried for 24 hours at 95°C ± 5°C. The sample was then crushed in a jaw crusher 
to 85%, -2 mm, and riffle split to produce an 800 g to 1 kg split for pulverisation and analysis. The sample was 
pulverised in a LM2 bowl (1 kg capacity) to 90% passing 75 μm.  
A minimum of 150 g to 300 g was scooped into a paper sample packet. All remaining pulp residues were put 
into new plastic sample bags and stored at the lab. The pulp in the sample packet was used for assay charges, 
and the residual materials are kept in the packet for storage. All sample preparation equipment is pre -
cleaned at the beginning of every sample with barren quartz prior to processing the samples. The laboratory 
provided crush and grind size reports for a range of samples in each batch. 
11.1.2 QAQC 
11.1.2.1 INTRODUCTION 
African Barrick Gold (ABG) maintained a comprehensive QAQC program for the project. Adequate validation 
and comparative analysis was completed to ensure that the historical drilling was equally representative of 
the gold grade distribution. Sample preparation, security and analysis meet mining industry requirements 
and are acceptable for resource estimation.  
Sample batches with QC failures were re -assayed with all failures addressed and documented in ABG’s 
acQuire® database. Standards were included in external checks to assist in ensuring laboratory accuracy and 
precision.  
Some poor precision was noted within the RC and DD core duplicates observed in the 2010-2012 data and 
can be attributed to the inherent variability within the deposit. Precision estimates for both preparation and 
pulp duplicates were good, indicating that the primary source of the poor precision must lie with the 
duplication of the field samples. While inc onsistent and/or inappropriate sampling techniques may have 
played a role, it is likely that the variability of the deposit is primarily responsible for the poor precision 
(nugget effect). An increase in frequency of duplicates was implemented for the high -grade mineralised 
zones of the deposit to better understand the precision issues. 
11.1.2.2 CRMs AND BLANKS 
The CRMs used in the Nyanzaga drilling programs are certified reference materials obtained from various 
sources. Different types of standards are used to cover low, intermediate and high-grade mineralisation in 
oxide and sulfide zones. If possible, a CRM was selected that is close in composition and grade to that of the 
samples contained in the batch. The buckets containing the reference material were kept in a clean, secure 
area in the exploration camp. Standards were inserted as prepared 150 to 200 g packets with each batch of 
samples. All samples were assayed in number sequence. 
Batch failures for accuracy and bias were defined as any assay result for a standard that is more or less than 
the value plus or minus three standard deviations, or any two consecutive values that are more or less than 
two standard deviations on the same side of the mean (bias). The mean and standard deviations for each

11.1.3 ASSAY METHODS 
Both SGS and ALS utilised fire assay techniques with a 50 g charge for the gold analysis with analysis codes 
of Au-AA24 and FAA505 respectively. The 50 g charge is mixed with flux and fused in clay crucibles. Lead 
buttons produced after fusions are cupelled and then digested in aqua regia. The digest is analysed for gold 
using atomic adsorption spectroscopy (AAS). The value is recorded electronically to the laboratory database, 
exported in csv format and emailed to the client for upload, followed by PDF copies of assay certificates.

12.1 SUMMARY 
Verification checks undertaken by the QP to confirm the validity of the Nyanzaga drilling database compiled 
for the current study include the following: 
• Checking for internal consistency between and within database tables. 
• Comparison of assay values between nearby holes. 
• Comparisons between assay results from different sampling phases. 
• Comparison of assay entries with laboratory source files. 
• Checks that surveyed locations of drill hole collars are within tolerance of proposed locations and 
locations recorded on field logging sheets. 
• Sense checks of down-hole surveys. 
• Checks for missing sample intervals, overlapping sample intervals, and duplicate sample numbers. 
• Comparisons of gold assays to visually logged intervals of alteration and mineralisation. 
• Visual comparisons, in cross-section and plan views, of gold grades and logged geology in neighbouring 
drill holes. 
 
These checks were undertaken using the compiled acQuire database implemented by Perseus. The QP’s 
database checks showed no significant inconsistencies. The available information indicates that the drilling 
database has been carefully compiled and validated, and in the QP’s opinion forms an appropriately reliable 
basis for the resource estimation included in the Report.

13. MINERAL PROCESSING AND METALLURGICAL TESTING  
This section of the report summarises metallurgical test work and predicted metallurgical performance of 
Nyanzaga Gold Project ores by ore type. Section 13.1 summarises historical metallurgical test work programs 
conducted before 2017. Section 13.2 summarises subsequent metallurgical test work programs conducted

the Kilimani deposit. Section 13.4 presents and discusses raw water analyses for the Project. Section 13.5 
summarises the predicted metallurgical performance for Nyanzaga Gold Project ores by ore type, based on

It is the opinion of the QP that metallurgical test work programs described in Section 13 are of sufficient 
scope and quality to support the production planning and the proposed process plant design described in

13.1 HISTORICAL METALLURGICAL TEST WORK 
The metallurgy of the Nyanzaga Gold Project was examined in six historical test work programs before 2017. 
These metallurgical investigations were commissioned by Barrick (Barrick Africa Corporation Limited, Barrick 
Exploration Africa Limited (BEAL) , Barrick Gold of Australia Limited  and African Barrick Gold plc ) and 
conducted by AMMTEC Ltd (AMMTEC) in Perth, Australia from 2005 to 2008 (AMMTEC Ltd, 2005); (AMMTEC 
Ltd, 2006); (AMMTEC Ltd, 2007a); (AMMTEC Ltd, 2007b); (AMMTEC Ltd, 2008) and JKTech Pty Ltd (JKTech) 
in Brisbane, Australia in 2012 (JKTech Pty Ltd, 2012). 
AMMTEC Ltd and JKTech Pty Ltd are commercial laboratories that are independent to Perseus. 
These historical metallurgical test work program s focused on the Nyanzaga deposit and determined the 
following: 
• Head assays and mineralogical examination indicated a relatively high degree of variability with regards 
to ore type and gold mineralisation. 
• Enrichment of mercury was noted in multiple samples. 
• The presence of fine/ultra fine gold occurrence was confirmed by diagnostic data. 
• Variable concentrations of coarse, gravity recoverable gold were noted, suggesting that some gold may 
be spotty in nature. Coarse, gravity gold recovery ranged from 7.7% to 51.4%, where measured. 
• The ore samples contained iron sulfides (pyrite, pyrrhotite) and iron oxides as their dominant mineral 
phases. Minor arsenopyrite was noted. Base metal sulfide content was relatively low. 
• It was noted that gold particles were present mostly as native gold and electrum, with an occurrence of 
aurostibnite (AuSb2) also noted. 
• A single molybdenum enriched sample was tested for rougher flotation response in the presence of 
potassium amyl xanthate (PAX) and Polyfroth® W55. Molybdenum recovery to rougher concentrate was 
poor (17.3% to 21.2%). Variable recovery to rougher concentrate was noted for gold (58.7% to 81.1%) 
and sulfur (64.6% to 89.4%) across the tests. 
• In direct cyanidation tests, g old extraction improved with increasing fineness of grind.  Moderate 
variability was noted across ore samples at the same grind size  (P80 of 106 µm) with regards to gold 
extraction (76.2% to 96.8% at 48 h) and reagent consumption levels (0.24 to 1.54 kg/t for lime (60% CaO) 
and 0.15 to 1.28 kg/t for NaCN). 
• Gold dissolution kinetics were rapid, with a significant amount of leaching completed within 8 h, and 
virtually all leaching completed within 24 h. 
• Although low levels of organic carbon were detected in some samples, direct leach and carbon-in-leach 
test work achieved similar gold extraction results, indicating that the Nyanzaga ore samples tested were 
not preg-robbing or preg-borrowing. NaCN consumptions were higher for CIL cyanidation tests than 
direct cyanidation tests.

13.2 NYANZAGA DEPOSIT TEST WORK 
The Nyanzaga deposit, as shown in Figure 16-3 and Figure 16-4, was the subject of test work programs 
commissioned by OreCorp, managed by Lycopodium, and conducted by SGS in Perth, Australia in 2016 and 
2017 (SGS, 2017), Outotec in Perth, Australia in 2017 (Outotec, 2017), and ALS Metallurgy in Perth, Australia 
in 2017 (ALS Metallurgy, 2017a), (ALS Metallurgy, 2017b). As noted in Section 15.2, the Nyanzaga deposit 
consists of 95% of tonnes and 96% of contained ounces of the Mineral Reserves for the Nyanzaga Gold 
Project. 
SGS, Outotec, and ALS Metallurgy are commercial laboratories that are independent to Perseus. 
Samples of oxide and fresh ore from the Nyanzaga deposit were tested to determine: 
• the most suitable processing route. 
• the plant operating parameters for Nyanzaga deposit ore types for the determined processing route, 
specifically throughput rate, gold recovery, and reagent consumption. 
• engineering parameters required for process plant design. 
The metallurgical test work program included the following: 
• comminution tests (SMC Test®, BWi and Ai on 20 comminution variability; CWi and RWi on three 
comminution variability samples; and UCS on 15 UCS variability samples). 
• ore type master composite test work program: 
• gold extraction test work to assess gravity, flotation and leaching characteristics across a range of 
process conditions, leading to selection and demonstration of an optimised extraction flowsheet and 
process conditions. 
• multi-stage diagnostic leach to gain understanding of gold deportment. 
• determination of parameters necessary for process plant design and operation (oxygen uptake rate). 
• engineering composite test work program: 
• bulk cyanidation tests, to provide samples for tailings testing (including mineralogical analysis). 
• determination of parameters necessary for process plant design and operation (viscosity, thickening 
and settling rate). 
• master composite test work program:

• arsenic precipitation test work. 
• determination of parameters necessary for process plant design and operation (carbon adsorption

• magnetic separation tests of 20 comminution variability samples. 
• BLEG tests on 30 BLEG variability samples to provide an indication of gold recovery by cyanidation. 
• gravity/cyanidation tests under optimised process conditions on 31 fresh ore metallurgical variability 
samples. 
13.2.1 SAMPLE SELECTION 
A total of 20 comminution variability samples, 15 UCS variability samples, 30 BLEG variability samples, 32 
metallurgical variability samples, four ore type composites, three engineering bulk composites and one 
master composite were selected from core taken from 57 drill holes spread across mineralised areas of the 
Nyanzaga deposit to provide spatial representivity. Samples were selected to focus the majority of test work 
on the four main ore types based on weathering (oxide) or member (mudstone (NMM), sandstone (NSM), 
or chert (NCM), as described in Figure 7-3). Samples were taken over an approximate range of: 
• 440 m east to west 
• 420 m north to south 
• 740 m in RL. 
Figures shown from Section  13.2.1.1 to Section 13.2.1.6 plot the metallurgical sample  intervals and the 
current pit shell design, as described in Section 16.1.2. It is noted in these Figures that s ome samples are 
located below the current pit shell, due to the fact that metallurgical test work samples selected for the 2017 
test work campaign considered both open pit and underground mine options.

13.2.2 HEAD GRADE AND SPECIFIC GRAVITY 
Each composite and metallurgical variability sample underwent fire assay  (FA) for gold in duplicate or 
triplicate, and multi-element analyses for a further 45 analytes (29 analytes for FR-ENG-PASTE). Metallurgical 
variability composites also underwent screen fire assay (SFA) for gold. Multi-element analyses were not  
conducted for OX-ENG-BULK, and FA for gold only was conducted on this composite. A summary of select 
assay results for composite and metallurgical variability samples is shown in Table 13-12. 
From the data presented: 
• It can be deduced that gold is present as both coarse spotty gold and fine gold in the Nyanzaga 
deposit. Coarse spotty gold is indicated by elevated screen fire assay values in the +75 µm fraction, 
when compared to the -75 µm fraction . The presence of the nuggety nature of some of the 
mineralisation was also noted in Section 11. Fine gold is indicated by consistency across FA and SFA 
total values, or where there are elevated screen fire assay values in the -75 µm fraction, when 
compared to the +75 µm fraction. 
• Silver is not present in an economic quantity, though it will need to be considered in process design 
for the CIL, elution, electrowinning and smelting circuits. Given the elevated silver grade in some 
samples, silver extraction was monitored in subsequent test work. 
• The sulfide sulfur assay data set indicates that sulfide minerals are present, even in some samples 
that were characterised as oxide. Metal speciation, combined with the m ineralogical analysis 
performed on the cyanidation leach residue of the fresh bulk engineering paste fill feed composite, 
presented in Section 13.2.7.1, suggests that the dominant sulfide mineral is pyrite, with pyrrhotite 
and arsenopyrite also present. This finding is also supported by low assay values across the data set 
for copper and base metals other than iron. Arsenic extraction was monitored in subsequent test 
work. 
• Organic carbon values are low for all samples except V-CH-FR-1, indicating that Nyanzaga deposit 
ore is unlikely to exhibit preg-robbing behaviour. 
• Mercury is present in most samples across all ore types – process design should consider options for 
mercury recovery and health monitoring of gold room personnel should be put into place to manage 
residual risk. Mercury extraction was monitored in subsequent test work. 
• Antimony levels are elevated across all ore types, increasing the risk of gold passivation that can 
occur at high pH. pH control should be included in the process control design. Antimony extraction 
was monitored in subsequent test work. 
• Tellurium assay levels are low, indicating that refractory telluride minerals are unlikely to be present.

13.2.4 FLOTATION 
As part of flowsheet definition test work, a series of tests were conducted on Nyanzaga deposit ore type 
composites (oxide, mudstone, sandstone, and chert) to determine the gold recovery response to  gravity 
concentration, flotation of gravity tailings, and cyanidation of flotation concentrate and tails streams. 
A summary of test work procedures used for flowsheet development and optimisation test work is included 
in Section 13.2.4.1 to Section 13.2.4.3. Results from the flowsheet development and optimisation test work 
are summarised in Section 13.2.4.4 to Section 13.2.4.6. An evaluation of the gravity/flotation/cyanidation 
flowsheet, compared to the gravity/cyanidation flowsheet, and selection of the preferred alternative is 
presented Section 13.2.15. 
13.2.4.1 GRAVITY SEPARATION TEST PROCEDURES 
Gravity separation test procedures were as described in Section 13.2.6.1.

143 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
13.2.4.2 FLOTATION TEST PROCEDURES 
In general, sighter flotation tests were conducted as follows: 
1. The flotation feed sample, prepared to a target P80 grind size in a stainless-steel laboratory rod mill, 
was transferred into a 5 L laboratory flotation cell. 
2. Perth tap water was added to slurrify the sample to establish the target pulp density (approximately 
33% w/w solids). 
3. The flotation feed cell, containing the sample slurry, was introduced to the Agitair laboratory 
flotation machine, with agitation speed set at 900 rpm. 
4. Copper sulfate was added (20 g/t) and the slurry was conditioned for 5 min. 
5. Further reagent additions were made to the pulp to achieve the desired pulp conditions and reagent 
concentrations. Dosing rates for the additional reagents were potassium amyl xanthate (135 g/t), 
Cytec® AERO® MAXGOLD® 900 promoter (30  g/t) and Huntsman POLYFROTH® W -22 frother (as 
required). All tests were conducted at natural pH. Adequate conditioning times were allowed after 
each addition (1-2 min per stage, for a total of 7 min additional conditioning time). 
6. Air was added, with the flow rate measured by a calibrated rotameter. 
7. Concentrate removal was performed under controlled conditions (50 mm scraper, operating at a 
10 s frequency) to ensure a consistent scrape frequency, and depth. Total flotation residence time 
was 30 min. 
8. Timed concentrates and the final flotation tails were filtered, dried at low temperature, and assayed 
for gold, silver, sulfur and sulfide sulfur. 
13.2.4.3 CYANIDATION TEST PROCEDURES 
Cyanidation of flotation concentrate and tails streams were performed as described in Section 13.2.6.2. 
13.2.4.4 GRAVITY/FLOTATION TESTS 
Four Nyanzaga ore type composites were subjected to two flotation amenability tests each under the 
following conditions: 
• Samples (4 kg) were prepared to grind size P80 of 125 µm and P80 of 75 µm. 
• Gravity separation was conducted on each grind size sample, with gravity concentrate treated by 
amalgamation (refer to Section 13.2.4.1). 
• Flotation tests were conducted on a reduced mass of 2 kg for each grind size sample (as described in 
Section 13.2.4.2). 
 
Three Nyanzaga fresh ore type composites (mudstone, sandstone and chert) were subjected to a further bulk 
flotation test, to generate sufficient mass of concentrate for subsequent cyanidation tests,  under the 
following conditions: 
• Samples (14 kg) were prepared to grind size P80 of 75 µm. 
• Gravity separation was conducted on each sample, with gravity concentrate treated by intensive 
cyanidation leach (refer to Section 13.2.4.1). 
• Flotation tests were conducted on a reduced mass of 4 kg (2× 2 kg flotation tests) for each grind size 
sample (as described in Section 13.2.4.2). 
 
The results from these gravity and flotation tests are presented in Table 13-25. Column headers prefixed with 
PW refer to the individual test numbers in the SGS report.

144 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
Key points from the gravity/flotation tests are: 
• Gold recovery to the gravity stage was highest for the oxide ore type composite (26.6% to 27.6%). Gold 
recovery to the gravity stage for the fresh ore type composites was 15.1% to 20.6% for mudstone, 20.5% 
to 21.4% for sandstone, and lowest for chert at 15.5% to 16.0%. 
• Gold recovery to the gravity stage was comparable across treatment methods (amalgamation and 
intensive cyanidation) for the same sample type at the same grind size. 
• In the flotation amenability tests, the fresh ore type composites recovered 82.5% to 95.1% of sulfides 
and 73.8% to 80.9% of gold in flotation feed to flotation concentrate, with 13.8% to 19.1% mass pull. 
• The oxide ore type composite performed poorer, recovering 75.4% to 79.9% of sulfides and 57.9% to 
61.4% of gold in flotation feed to flotation concentrate, with 9.4% to 11.6% mass pull. 
• The oxide and chert ore type composites observed higher gold recovery at the finer grind size (P 80 of 
75 µm vs P 80 of 125  µm), but mudstone and sandstone ore type composites observed higher gold 
recovery at the coarser grind size. 
• Gold flotation kinetics were similar for all ores, with approximately 90% of the gold recovered to flotation 
concentrate occurring in the first six minutes. 
• The bulk flotation tests showed similar sulfide and gold recoveries across all fresh ore type composites, 
with 89.3% to 92.5 % of sulfides  and 78.1% to 80.2% of gold present in flotation feed recovered to 
flotation concentrate. Mass pulls were also comparable, at 13.8% to 16.7%. 
• Combined gold recovery (gravity and flotation) was 75.1% to 80.6% for the fresh ores , and 64.9% to 
69.1% for oxide ore, indicating that flotation won’t be able to produce an economic throw away tailings 
stream.

13.2.4.6 CYANIDATION OF FLOTATION PRODUCTS 
Following flotation, cyanide leach tests were performed on bulk flotation concentrates under the following 
conditions:

• Direct cyanidation of the flotation concentrate samples was conducted (as per Section 13.2.4.3), with the 
following parameters: 
• 250 g sample tested. 
• Pulp density of 30% w/w solids. 
• Pre-oxidation step performed. 
• Sodium cyanide addition of 3 kg/t, maintain above 0.1% w/v. 
• 72 h leach time. 
 
Cyanide leach tests were also performed on bulk flotation tails under the following conditions: 
• Flotation tails, at P80 of 75 µm, was received from the bulk flotation tests. 
• Direct cyanidation of the samples was conducted ( as per Section 13.2.4.3), with the following 
parameters: 
• 1,000 g sample tested. 
• Pulp density of 40% w/w solids. 
• No pre-oxidation step performed. 
• Sodium cyanide addition of 1.5 kg/t, maintain above 0.03% w/v. 
• 20 g/L of activated carbon for mudstone ore type composite flotation tailings sample only, as per the

13.2.5 BLEG TEST WORK 
Thirty variability samples were subjected to BLEG tests  to provide an indication of gold recovery by 
cyanidation. Duplicate tests were conducted at two separate laboratory facilities. BLEG test conditions were: 
• Approximately 1,000 g of solids were used for the first batch of tests, and approximately 500 g of solids 
were used for the second batch of tests. 
• Samples were pulverised. Although not measured or stated in the laboratory test work report, a typical 
grind size of 95% passing 75 µm (P95 of 75 µm) can be considered. 
• Samples were slurrified to 50% w/w solids using Perth tap supply  
• pH established and maintained within a range of 10.5 to 11.0, using hydrated lime. 
• Initial NaCN concentration of 0.25% w/w. 
• Oxygen sparged into the bottle head space, to maintain DO concentrations above 20 mg/L. 
• 24 h bottle roll cyanidation, with gold and silver analysis of solid residue. 
 
Note that as the samples are pulverised to  a finer particle size distribution that the optimised 
gravity/cyanidation test conditions (P80 of 75 µm, as noted in Section  13.2.6.4), gold extractions may be 
overstated. The leach time for the BLEG tests, at 24  h, is  the same residence time selected from 
gravity/cyanidation tests (as noted in Section 13.2.6.3). The sodium cyanide concentration used is higher 
than the range tested in gravity/cyanidation tests (as noted in Section 13.2.6.7). The results of the tests are 
summarised in Table 13-27. The calculated head grade was derived by an addition of the cyanide recoverable 
portion of the sample plus the leach solid residue grade. 
Key points from the data are: 
• Generally good correlation between test 1 and test 2 calculated gold grades, though the calculated gold 
grades are approximately 10% lower than the sextuplicate fire assay gold head grades. 
• Generally good correlation between test  1 and test  2 gold extraction. Moderate variability in gold 
extraction was noted across samples. 
• There was poor correlation between test 1 and test 2 calculated silver grades (approximately 30% higher 
on average for test 1 compared to test 2) and silver extractions (test 2 extractions approximately double 
test 1 extractions on average). This may indicate slow leaching silver components of the ore, as well as 
BLEG leach conditions being sub-optimal for silver extraction. 
• BLEG gold extractions for oxide samples range between 86.2% and 95.3%, with an average of 91.1%. 
• BLEG gold extractions for mudstone samples range between 73.6% and 93.2%, with an average of 85.5%. 
• BLEG gold extractions for sandstone samples range between 74.6% and 94.3%, with an average of 88.6%. 
• BLEG gold extractions were the lowest for the chert samples, with a range between 33.9% and 97.1% 
and an average of 78.9% (excludes one test that reported 0% extraction). It is uncertain whether low test 
results were due to procedural issues, insufficient leach reagent(s) for the reaction (e.g., oxygen), or preg-
robbing effects. 
• BLEG gold extractions for axial fault samples range between 83.3% and 92.0%, with an average of 87.8%. 
• BLEG gold extractions for all ore types, except chert, correlate with the data range observed for 
metallurgical variability samples under optimised gravity/cyanidation conditions (Section  13.2.6.11). 
BLEG gold extractions for chert samples RCBT95381 and RCBT95664 fall significantly below the range 
observed for metallurgical variability samples of this ore type under optimised gravity/cyanidation 
conditions. 
• BLEG silver extractions across ore types ranged between 5.9% and 94.0%, with an average of 47.8%.

13.2.6 GRAVITY RECOVERY AND CYANIDATION 
As part of flowsheet definition test work, a series of tests were conducted on Nyanzaga deposit ore type 
composites (oxide, mudstone, sandstone, and chert) to determine the gold recovery response to gravity 
recovery and cyanidation. A further objective was to optimise gold recovery through testing and evaluating 
a range of gravity recovery and cyanidation conditions.

153 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
A summary of test work procedures used for flowsheet development and optimisation test work is included 
in Section 13.2.6.1 to Section 13.2.6.2. Results from the flowsheet development and optimisation test work 
are summarised in Section  13.2.6.3 to Section 13.2.6.7. Results from demonstration and bulk tests are 
presented in Section 13.2.6.8 and Section 13.2.6.9. The optimised gravity/cyanidation test conditions are 
collated in Section 13.2.6.10. Results from test work conducted on metallurgical variability samples at the 
optimised gravity/leach test conditions are summarised in Section  13.2.6.11. An evaluation of the 
gravity/cyanidation flowsheet, compared to the gravity/flotation/cyanidation flowsheet, and selection of the 
preferred alternative is presented Section 13.2.15. 
13.2.6.1 GRAVITY SEPARATION TEST PROCEDURES 
In general, gravity recovery tests were conducted as follows: 
1. The gravity feed sample, prepared to a target P80 grind size in a stainless steel laboratory rod mill, 
was passed through a 3-inch laboratory Knelson gravity concentrator. 
2. The gravity concentrate and tail streams were then processed via one of the following processes: 
a. The gravity concentrate (60 g to 90 g) was transferred to a 2 L leach bottle with a screw-on 
lid and slurrified to approximately 30% w/w solids with Perth tap water. 10 g of mercury was 
added to the bottle, along with 0.1 g of NaOH, and the bottle was continuously rolled for 2 h 
to 3 h. On completion of the amalgamation, the loaded amalgam was recovered by hand 
panning and assayed for gold. The combined gravity/amalgam tail were then combined and 
oven dried at low temperature (70 °C), and then processed via the flotation procedure 
(Section 13.2.4.2) or the cyanidation procedure (Section 13.2.6.2). 
b. The gravity concentrate (60 g to 90 g) was hand panned to reduce mass to approximately 
50 g and transferred to a 2 L leach bottle with a screw-on lid and slurrified to approximately 
10% w/w solids with Perth tap water . 1.0 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) with 1.5  g of 
LeachAid were then added prior to sodium cyanide (NaCN) addition to a concentration of 
1.5% w/v. On completion of the 24 h intensive leach, the solution was assayed for gold and 
silver. The combined gravity/intensive cyanidation tail were then combined and oven dried 
at low temperature (70°C), and then processed via the flotation procedure (Section 13.2.4.2) 
or the cyanidation procedure (Section 13.2.6.2). 
13.2.6.2 CYANIDATION TEST PROCEDURES 
In general, cyanidation tests were conducted as follows: 
1. The cyanidation feed sample, prepared to a target P80 grind size in a stainless steel laboratory rod 
mill, was transferred into a leach bottle (typically 5 L capacity) with a screw-on lid. 
2. Perth tap water was added to slurrify the sample to establish the target pulp density (% w/w solids). 
3. If a pre-oxidation step was being performed, hydrated lime (60% w/w CaO) was added to the slurry 
to establish pH of 10.5. The headspace of the leach bottle was filled with oxygen or air to achieve a 
target DO concentration, or oxygen or air was sparged to the leach bottle, and the bottle was placed 
on the bottle rolls for 2 h, with slurry agitation applied by mechanical rollers. If a pre-oxidation step 
was not required, then Step 3 was skipped and the test proceeded to Step 4. 
4. If a carbon-in-leach test was being performed, activated carbon (Haycarb YAO 8×16) was added to 
the required concentration. Otherwise, if a direct cyanidation test was being performed, then Step 4 
was skipped and the test proceeded to Step 5. 
5. Hydrated lime (60% w/w CaO) was added to the slurry to adjust pH into the range of 10.0 to 10.5. 
6. Sodium cyanide was added to the slurry to establish the target initial cyanide concentration. 
7. The headspace of the leach bottle was filled with oxygen or air to provide an elevated DO content, 
or oxygen or air was sparged to the leach bottle.

154 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
8. The leach bottle was placed on the bottle rolls. Slurry agitation was applied by mechanical rollers. 
9. At regular intervals, slurry pH, DO, and sodium cyanide concentration were monitored and recorded. 
Solution sub-samples were taken and assayed for gold and silver. Additional mercury and arsenic 
assays were performed for selected tests. 
10. If required during the test duration, lime, sodium cyanide and oxygen/air were added to maintain 
target levels. pH was maintained above 10.0 and DO was maintained above the target level for the 
test. 
11. At the conclusion of the test, the terminal pH, oxygen, and cyanide levels were determined. A 
solution sub-sample was taken and assayed for gold  and silver. The residual slurry sample was 
filtered, washed, and dried to provide leach residue solids, and a sub-sample of residue solid was 
assayed for gold and silver. Where applicable, carbon was extracted, rinsed, and dried, and a sub-
sample was assayed for gold and silver. Additional arsenic, mercury and antimony assays were 
performed on final liquors and test residues for selected tests. The levels of CNWAD, OCN- and SCN- 
were also measured in final liquors for selected tests. 
13.2.6.3 DIRECT CYANIDATION AND CIL COMPARISON 
To assess the potential for preg-robbing or preg-borrowing behaviour, samples of the Nyanzaga ore type 
composites were subjected to 48 h leach tests. The first type of test was a direct cyanide leach , and the 
second type of test was a carbon-in-leach test. 
The tests were conducted under the following conditions: 
• 1,000 g sample tested. 
• Grind size P80 of 75 µm. 
• No gravity separation. 
• No pre-oxygenation. 
• Pulp density of 40% w/w solids. 
• Initial NaCN concentration of 0.10% w/v, maintained at 0.03% w/v. 
• No activated carbon addition for direct cyanidation tests; 20 g/L activated carbon addition for CIL tests. 
 
The results of these tests are summarised in Table 13-28. Column headers prefixed with PW refer to the 
individual test numbers in the SGS report. 
Key findings from the tests are: 
• 48 h gold extractions varied between 81.8% and 93.1%. 
• Gold leach kinetics for all ore type composites were rapid, with most of the recoverable gold extracted 
within the first eight hours. Silver leach kinetics for the fresh ore type composites were slower than for 
the oxide ore type composite, with leaching still occurring after 24 h. Silver leaching in the oxide ore type 
composite was largely complete within 12 h. Based on these observations, a CIL residence time of 24 h 
was selected for plant design. 
• Assays on final liquor indicated that between 11% and 30% of mercury was solubilised during the 48 h 
leach. Trace amounts of arsenic and antimony were also detected in leach solutions for the oxide ore 
type composite, increasing up to 10-18 ppm As and 6 ppm Sb for fresh ore type composites. 
• Sodium cyanide consumptions were low (0.15 kg/t to 0.58 kg/t for direct cyanidation tests and 0.79 kg/t 
to 0.93 kg/t for CIL tests) and lime consumptions were moderate (1.10 kg/t to 1.58 kg/t). 
• For oxide, sandstone and chert ore type composites, residue grades are comparable for each sample 
between direct cyanidation and CIL tests, indicating negligible preg-robbing or preg-borrowing.

155 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
• For the mudstone ore type composite, the residue grades for the CIL test are significantly lower  (by 
0.10 g/t Au) and the gold recovery in significantly higher (6.0%) than for the direct cyanidation test. This 
indicates that either preg-borrowing or minor preg-robbing is occurring for this sample, and that the 
activity of the carbon is sufficient to compete with these observed effects. 
• For future cyanidation tests, it is recommended that oxide, sandstone and chert samples be subjected to 
direct cyanidation and mudstone samples will be subjected to CIL tests, unless additional confirmatory 
testing is performed.

13.2.6.4 GRIND SIZE OPTIMISATION AND COMPARISON OF CYANIDATION AND 
GRAVITY/CYANIDATION 
To assess the effect of grind size on gold extraction , samples of the Nyanzaga ore type composites were 
subjected to leach tests with durations of 24 h (to 32  h). To assess the benefits of inclusion of a gravity 
recovery step before cyanidation, the fresh ore type composites were tested at each grind size both with and 
without a gravity concentration step prior to cyanidation. The oxide ore type composite was tested at each 
grind size with a gravity concentration step prior to cyanidation only. 
The tests were conducted under the following conditions: 
• 1,000 g sample tested in cyanidation. 
• Inclusion of gravity extraction using amalgamation, as noted above. 
• No pre-oxygenation step. Target DO of 20 ppm using oxygen gas. 
• Pulp density of 40% w/w solids. 
• Initial NaCN concentration of 0.10% w/v, maintained at 0.03% w/v. 
• No activated carbon addition  for oxide, sandstone and chert ore type composites; 20 g/L activated 
carbon addition for tests on the mudstone ore type composite; for the mudstone ore type composite at 
grind size P80 of 75 µm only, additional tests were conducted with no activated carbon to confirm the 
results and conclusions from Section 13.2.6.3. 
• Grind sizes tested were P80 of 125, 106, 75 and 53 µm. 
 
The results of these tests are summarised in Table 13-29 and Table 13-30. Column headers prefixed with PW 
refer to the individual test numbers in the SGS report. 
Key findings from the tests are: 
• All ore type composites tested were grind sensitive  with respect to gold , with gold extraction rates 
increasing with decreasing grind size.  This was observed for tests both with an d without a gravity 
recovery step. 
• When comparing like-for-like flowsheet tests on the same ore type composite  at varying grind sizes, 
reagent consumptions are relatively consistent between grind size P80 of 125 µm and P80 of 75 µm, but 
lime and/or cyanide consumption increases at the finer grind size P80 of 53 µm. 
• Mercury, arsenic and antimony concentrations in the leach solution did not vary with grind size, 
indicating that these elements are not grind sensitive. 
• Techno-economic assessment determined that grind size P80 of 75 µm was optimal, and this was used 
for further test work and process plant design. Sharp decreases in recovery were noted at grind sizes 
coarser than P80 of 75 µm, and the value of the incremental gold extracted grinding finer to P80 of 53 µm 
did not offset the additional incremental capital cost and incremental operating cost associated with 
grinding energy and reagent dosing. 
• Gravity recoveries were consistently replicated across multiple tests performed on the same ore type 
composites, as well as correlating with the ore type composite gravity recoveries noted in 
Section 13.2.4.4. 
• Marginally lower residue grades were achieved for tests that included a gravity recovery stage before 
cyanidation. 
• Except for one data pair, reagents consumptions are marginally lower for tests with a preceding gravity 
recovery stage compared to cyanidation only tests. This effect is most pronounced for the sandstone ore 
type composite.

158 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
• Techno-economic assessment determined a marginal benefit for including a gravity recovery stage 
before cyanidation. At full plant scale, including a gravity circuit in the process flowsheet will also reduce 
the impact of coarse free gold on cyanidation performance and regulate plant feed grade, enabling more 
stable operation of CIL and elution circuits. Intensive cyanidation of gravity concentrate may also realise 
improved leaching of gold associated with semi-refractory minerals that may be present. Furthermore, 
removing any coarse gold components early in the process flowsheet is advantageous in terms of 
security. Therefore, gravity recovery was used as a standard parameter for plant design and all further 
test work, unless otherwise noted. 
• The preg-borrowing properties of mudstone ore observed in Section 13.2.6.3 were also noted in the 
paired tests with no preceding gravity recovery stage in Section 13.2.6.4.

TECHNICAL REPORT

To evaluate the effect of various oxidising conditions on gold extraction, samples of the Nyanzaga ore type 
composites were subjected to leach tests with durations of 24  h. The tests were conducted under the 
following conditions: 
• 1,000 g sample tested in cyanidation. 
• Grind size P80 of 75 µm. 
• Inclusion of gravity extraction using amalgamation. 
• Pulp density of 40% w/w solids. 
• Initial NaCN concentration of 0.10% w/v, maintained at 0.03% w/v.

carbon addition for tests on the mudstone ore type composite.

• Dissolved oxygen (DO) levels controlled with oxygen head space in the leach bottle,  with 3 h of pre -
oxygenation performed prior to leach, targeting DO ≥20 ppm. 
• DO levels maintained by aeration only, with 3 h of pre-aeration performed prior to leach, targeting DO 
in the range of 5 ppm to 10 ppm. 
• Dissolved oxygen (DO) levels controlled with oxygen head space in the leach bottle, targeting DO 
≥20 ppm, with 100 g/t of lead nitrate added prior to leach.

• Higher DO levels, from the addition of oxygen gas, result in lower residue gold grades.

• Controlling DO with oxygen head space in the leach bottle, targeting DO ≥20  ppm, was selected for

13.2.6.8 DEMONSTRATION TESTS AT OPTIMISED CONDITIONS 
To verify the optimised gravity/cyanidation conditions for Nyanzaga ores, a series of 22 demonstration leach 
tests were conducted. Most sets of conditions were tested in duplicate, except as otherwise noted. 
For the Nyanzaga fresh ore type composites and the Nyanzaga master composite, the effectiveness of gravity 
extraction was examined through tests both with and without gravity extraction before cyanidation. For the 
Nyanzaga oxide ore type composite, tests with gravity extraction only were performed. 
The tests were conducted under the following conditions:

13.2.6.10 NYANZAGA DEPOSIT OPTIMISED GRAVITY/CYANIDATION TEST PROCEDURE 
The following optimised gravity/leach test conditions were carried forward for testing of the Nyanzaga Gold 
Project metallurgical variability samples: 
1. Approximately 2,000 g of gravity feed sample, prepared to a P 80 of 75  µm in a stainless steel 
laboratory rod mill, was passed through a 3-inch laboratory Knelson gravity concentrator. 
2. The gravity concentrate (60 g to 90 g) was hand panned to reduce mass to approximately 50 g and 
transferred to a 2 L leach bottle with a screw-on lid and slurrified to approximately 10% w/w solids 
with Perth tap water. 1.0 g of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) with 1.5 g of LeachAid was then added prior 
to sodium cyanide (NaCN) addition to a concentration of 1.5%  w/v. On completion of the 24  h 
intensive leach, the solution was assayed for gold and silver. The combined gravity/intensive 
cyanidation tail were then combined and oven dried at low temperature (70°C). 
3. A 1,000 g sub-sample was taken, and the  cyanidation feed was transferred into a leach bottle  
(typically 5 L capacity) with a screw -on lid. Perth tap water was added to slurrify the sample to 
establish 50% w/w solids.

173 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
4. For mudstone samples, or composites containing m udstone ore, activated carbon (Haycarb YAO 
8×16) was added to the required concentration. Otherwise, all other samples types were subjected 
to direct cyanidation tests, and Step 4 was skipped and the test proceeded to Step 5. 
5. Hydrated lime (60% w/w CaO) was added to the slurry to establish pH in the range of 10.0 to 10.5. 
6. Sodium cyanide was added to the slurry to establish the target initial concentration of 0.050% w/v. 
7. The headspace of the leach bottle was filled with oxygen, or oxygen was sparged to the leach bottle, 
to achieve an elevated DO concentration of 20 ppm. 
8. The leach bottle was placed on the bottle rolls. Slurry agitation was applied by mechanical rollers. 
9. At regular intervals, slurry pH, DO, and sodium cyanide concentration were monitored and recorded. 
Solution sub-samples were taken and assayed for gold and silver. 
10. If required during the test duration, lime, sodium cyanide and oxygen were added to maintain target 
levels. Target pH range to maintain was 10.0 to 10.5; target NaCN concentration to maintain was 
0.010% w/v, and target DO to maintain was 20 ppm. 
11. At the conclusion of the 24 h test, the terminal pH, oxygen, and cyanide levels were determined. A 
solution sub-sample was taken and assayed for gold and silver. The residual slurry sample was 
filtered, washed, and dried to provide leach residue solids, and a sub-sample of residue solid was 
assayed for gold and silver. Where applicable, carbon was extracted, rinsed, and dried, and a sub-
sample was assayed for gold and silver. Additional arsenic, mercury and antimony assays were 
performed on final liquors and test residues.

13.2.7.1 MULTI-STAGE DIAGNOSTIC LEACH 
Sub-samples of fresh ore type composites (mudstone, sandstone and chert), ground to a P80 of 75 µm, were 
subjected to multi-stage diagnostic leach tests to determine the deportment of gold. The stages of the test 
are summarised as follows:  
1. The ground ore was passed through a laboratory Knelson gravity concentrator and the concentrate 
amalgamated with 5 g of mercury. The amalgam was submitted for gold assay. 
2. After recovery of the mercury amalgam, the combined tailings (amalgamation tails and gravity 
concentrator tails) were subjected to a standard cyanide leach. The final liquor and residue were 
sub-sampled and submitted for gold assay. 
3. The remaining cyanidation residue was then subjected to a dilute HCl digest at 60°C for 4 h. The final 
pulp was filtered and the residue thoroughly washed. The final liquor and residue were sub-sampled 
and submitted for gold assay. A standard cyanide leach was conducted on the remaining HCl digest 
residue, and samples of the leach liquor and residue submitted for assay. 
4. A dilute nitric acid leach test (25% HNO3 at 80°C for 4 h) was conducted on the remaining residue 
from step 3. The final liquor and residue were sub-sampled and submitted for gold assay. A standard 
cyanide leach was conducted on the remaining HCl digest residue, and samples of the leach liquor 
and residue submitted for assay. 
5. The leach residue was analysed for gold by fire assay and aqua regia digest. The difference between 
fire assay (total gold) and aqua regia digest ( sulfide, or non -silicate occluded gold) results was 
considered to be silicate/gangue ± graphitic carbon encapsulated gold.

13.2.8 CARBON ADSORPTION KINETICS 
The adsorption of precious metal species from solution by activated carbon in a continuous carbon-in-pulp 
(CIP) adsorption train generally obeys the following empirically derived relationship: 
∆[𝑀]𝐶 = 𝑘. [𝑀]𝑆. 𝑡𝑛 
Where: 
• Δ[M]C = Change in the concentration of the precious metal on carbon since time t=0 (in mg/L). 
• k = Empirical rate constant dependent upon slurry mixing efficiency, pulp viscosity and carbon particle 
size (in h-1). 
• [M]S = Equilibrium concentration of the precious metal in solution (in mg/L) 
• t = Elapsed time (in h) 
• n = Exponential constant relating to the loading capacity specific to the precious metal (typically in the 
range of 0.5 to 1.2). 
Although the above model was derived for continuous CIP systems, experience has shown that indicative 
values of k and n (referred to as Fleming gold adsorption constants) can be determined by applying regression 
analysis to data from the first hours of a sequential batch CIP test. Slurry from Nyanzaga master composite 
bulk leach test PW3396 (refer to Section 13.2.6.9) was subjected to sequential triple-contact CIP leach test

13.2.10.2 HYDROGEN PEROXIDE CYANIDE DETOXIFICATION 
Cyanide detoxification using hydrogen peroxide was undertaken on Nyanzaga fresh bulk engineering paste 
fill feed composite cyanidation tailings slurry at 50% w/w solids concentration from bulk leach tests JR2930 
and JR2931 (refer to Section 13.2.6.8). 30% w/w hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) solution was added as the oxidant 
and copper sulfate pentahydrate (CuSO 4.5H2O) was added as a catalyst for the cyanide detoxification 
reaction. 
Residual NaCN concentrations of between 0.008% and 0.015% were reported after 24  h of leach  in the 
cyanide detoxification feed sample. CNWAD concentrations in solution post-cyanidation were not reported. 
Although CNWAD and CNfree concentrations were not quantified in the ALS Metallurgy report after the cyanide 
detoxification step, it was noted after a 30 min reaction time than no remaining free cyanide was detected 
by titration. It has been back-calculated from available test work notes that an 800% stoichiometric ratio of 
H2O2 to CNfree was added to achieve no detectable free cyanide after 30 min reaction time across these two 
tests. 
150% to 300% stoichiometric ratio of H2O2 to CNWAD is typical in the gold mining industry. It is noted that 
excess oxidant was added for these tests to ensure that no remaining free cyanide was detectable, given that

13.2.15 PROCESSING ROUTE SELECTION 
A techno -economic assessment of the following three process ing routes was conducted to select the 
optimum flowsheet for treating Nyanzaga deposit ores: 
• Gravity, flotation, cyanidation of flotation concentrate, and cyanidation of flotation tailings – all stages 
with target grind size P80 of 75 µm (Section 13.2.4.4 and Section 13.2.4.6). 
• Gravity (P80 of 75 µm), flotation (P80 of 75 µm), regrind and cyanidation of flotation concentrate (P100 of 
25 µm), and cyanidation of flotation tailings (P80 of 75 µm) (Section 13.2.4.4 and Section 13.2.4.6). 
• Gravity and cyanidation – all stages with target grind size P80 of 75 µm (Section 13.2.6.8). 
 
Key findings of the technical assessment were: 
• The highest gold recovery is achieved with gravity, flotation, regrind and cyanidation of flotation 
concentrate, and cyanidation of flotation tailings. This process route also has the highest incremental 
capital cost (associated with flotation, regrind, concentrate thickening, an additional flotation 
concentrate CIL circuit, and additional reagent mixing facilities)  and the highest incremental 
operating cost (additional power, reagents and consumables, labour, and maintenance). 
• For both processing routes involving flotation, the incremental capital and operating costs were not 
offset by the projected revenue from additional precious metal production. 
• The gravity and cyanidation processing route has a minor trade -off in gold recovery , but has no  
incremental capital and operating cost considerations, compared to the two flowsheet options  
involving flotation. 
 
Based on this techno-economic assessment, and the findings of test work from Section 13.2 of this report, 
the following process flowsheet was selected for plant design:

• Target grind size P80 of 75 µm. 
• Gravity recovery. 
• Pre-oxygenation (target DO of 20 ppm through the addition of oxygen gas). 
• Carbon-in-leach (with target pH of 10.0-10.5, and target DO of 20 ppm through the addition of oxygen 
gas). 
 
Sodium cyanide and lime addition rates are ore type dependent and have been estimated in Section 13.5.3.

13.3.6.1 GRAVITY/CYANIDATION TEST PROCEDURE 
The following gravity/cyanidation test conditions were used for testing of the Kilimani deposit metallurgical 
variability samples: 
1. Approximately 2,000 g of gravity feed sample, prepared to a P 80 of 75  µm in a stainless steel 
laboratory rod mill, was passed through a 3-inch laboratory Knelson gravity concentrator (KC-MD3) 
with a 0.12 kW drive, operating at 1,500 rpm with 3.5 L/min fluidisation water addition. 
2. The gravity concentrate was transferred to a 1 L leach bottle with a screw-on lid. 10 g of mercury 
was added to the bottle, along with 0.1 g of NaOH, and the bottle was continuously rolled for 2 to 
3 h. On completion of the amalgamation, the loaded amalgam was recovered by hand panning and 
assayed for gold. The combined gravity/amalgam tail were then combined and oven dried. 
3. A 1,000 g sub-sample was taken, and the cyanidation feed was transferred into a 4 L leach bottle 
with a screw-on lid. Perth tap water was added to slurrify the sample to establish the 40% w/w solids. 
4. No activated carbon is added to the cyanidation slurry. 
5. Hydrated lime (68% w/w CaO) was added to the slurry to establish pH in the range of 10.0 to 10.5. 
6. Sodium cyanide was added to the slurry to establish the target initial concentration of 0.100% w/w. 
7. Oxygen was sparged to the leach bottle to achieve an elevated DO concentration of 20 ppm. 
8. The leach bottle was placed on the bottle rolls. Slurry agitation was applied by mechanical rollers. 
9. At regular intervals, slurry pH, DO, and sodium cyanide concentration were monitored and recorded. 
Solution sub-samples were taken and assayed for gold and silver. 
10. If required during the test duration, lime, sodium cyanide, and oxygen were added to maintain target 
levels. Target pH range to maintain was >10.0; target NaCN concentration to maintain was 
0.030% w/w, and target DO to maintain was 20 ppm. 
11. At the conclusion of the 48 h test, the terminal pH, oxygen, and cyanide levels were determined. A 
solution sub-sample was taken and assayed for gold and silver. The residual slurry sample was

197

filtered, washed, and dried to provide leach residue solids, and a sub-sample of residue solid was 
assayed for gold and silver.

It is noted from a detailed review of the data set to determine sodium cyanide consumption and lime addition 
rates, that tests including a gravity recovery stage could result in biasing of reagent consumptions. In the case

13.6 DELETERIOUS ELEMENTS 
The Nyanzaga and Kilimani deposit ores contain elevated concentrations of mercury, arsenic and antimony. 
It is noted that some ore samples also contained detectable concentrations of organic carbon. 
In general, mercury, arsenic and antimony concentrations in test work leach solutions did not vary with grind 
size, indicating that the solubility of these elements is not grind sensitive. Extraction of these elements was 
noted to increase with increasing cyanide concentration in leach. At optimised cyanide concentrations, leach 
tailings solutions reported indicative concentrations of 6-13 ppm As and 4-6 ppm Sb. Mercury was noted to 
preferentially load onto the activated carbon in CIL tests. Comparison tests between direct cyanidation and 
CIL indicated that negligible preg-robbing or preg-borrowing occurred for most ore types, and for Nyanzaga 
deposit mudstone ores, the activity of carbon in CIL is sufficient to compete with observed preg-borrowing 
effects. The preg-borrowing effects observed for Nyanzaga deposit mudstone ores may be due to organic 
carbon, or due to the presence of fine-grained iron oxides or clay minerals (due to surface adsorption). 
The process design includes a mercury handling circuit, due to the low-level presence of mercury across the 
Nyanzaga ore types, to mitigate the health hazards associated with mercury exposure. Provision has been 
made in sustaining capital for a water treatment plant should arsenic  or antimony present operational 
challenges in the future. pH control is included in the process control design to mitigate gold passivation that 
can occur at high pH due to elevated antimony levels. 
Test work and modelling indicates that organic carbon, soluble arsenic and soluble antimony will not have a 
significant effect on potential economic recovery of gold in a carbon-in-leach cyanidation process. It is noted 
that soluble arsenic and soluble antimony will be contained within the tailings and process water systems.

14.1 OVERVIEW 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project Mineral Resource estimate consists of two discrete but adjacent  deposits: 
Nyanzaga and Kilimani. The data cut-off date for this latest resource update is September 1, 2024. Mineral 
Resources are inclusive of Mineral Reserves. 
Geological and mineralisation wireframes and the estimation for the Nyanzaga resource model were 
prepared by Mr Daniel Saunders, as an employee of Perseus in the role of Group Resource Geologist Business 
Growth. Mr Saunders assumes responsibility for the Mineral Resource estimates disclosed in this report. 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project Mineral Resource estimate has an Effective Date of October 1, 2024 and has been 
disclosed in accordance with NI 43-101 and prepared using the CIM Definition Standards and CIM Best 
Practice Guidelines. This Report summarises the work completed by Perseus to prepare the Mineral Resource 
models and Mineral Resource estimates. 
Previous (historical) Mineral Resource estimates for the Nyanzaga Gold Project are described in Section 6. 
14.2 METHODS SUMMARY 
Mineral Resources reported herein have been estimated using a geostatistical block modelling approach, 
informed from gold assay data obtained from predominantly core and RC drill chip samples. The geological 
wireframes consider structural and lithological interpretations of the gold mineralisation. 
The Nyanzaga Mineral Resource estimate used Seequent Leapfrog Geo software for the geological and 
mineralisation interpretation and associated drill hole coding, while Maptek Vulcan software was used for 
block model creation, editing and reporting. The grade interpolation of the Nyanzaga component of the 
resource model was completed in Isatis, with the ordinary kriged estimates for Kilimani completed in Vulcan. 
The evaluation of the Nyanzaga Mineral Resource involved the following procedures: 
• Database compilation and verification. 
• Generation and verification of three-dimensional geological models. 
• Data conditioning (including compositing and grade capping), statistical analysis and variography. 
• Selection of estimation strategies and estimation parameters. 
• Block model generation, grade estimation and validation. 
• Mineral Resource classification. 
• Preparation of the Mineral Resource estimate and reporting.

14.4 GEOLOGICAL INTERPRETATION AND MODELLING 
14.4.1 LITHOLOGY INTERPRETATION 
The lithological model of the Nyanzaga Gold Project Mineral Resource was constructed with consideration 
of the stratigraphic sequence originally defined by ABG and updated by OreCorp as outlined in Section 7.2. 
The drill hole data coded with the respective member units  used for the 2017 estimate (referred to as 
“cycles”) were imported into Leapfrog along with the other drill hole information. 
The members were then assessed spatially and adjustments made to the coding to generate consistent units 
across the block model area.  Where available , structural data reflecting bedding obs ervations w ere 
incorporated into the lithology model to guide the locations of folding, particularly the interpreted anticlinal

14.4.2 STRUCTURAL MODELLING 
The Nyanzaga Mineral Resource block model was built on the basis of  fault blocks which were used to 
separate faulted portions of the model. The 2017 Mineral Resource included interpretations for 19 individual 
faults. Some of these were interpreted to extend across the entire deposit, while others were modelled as 
relatively local features. The revised interpretation completed by Perseus assessed these faults against direct 
evidence of their location, such as mapped outcrop positions, or inferred by changes in the stratigraphic 
sequence (thickness, repetitions etc.). This resulted in a simplified fault model for the project which utilised 
seven different faults, with the assigned interaction priorities of each generating 16 individual fault blocks. A 
representation of the faults is presented Figure 14-4. 
The two most significant faults, with respect to the lithology and mineralisation interpretation, are the axial 
fault (AF) and the far east fault (FF1). The AF has previously been interpreted to host structural controlled 
mineralisation associated with brecciation. The FF1 is significant as it serves to terminate the extension of

14.4.3.1 NYANZAGA DEPOSIT 
Mineralisation at the Nyanzaga Gold Project is interpreted as a combination of lithology hosted within 
favourable units, and structurally hosted associated with faulting and associated brittle zones. As a result of

difficult, and attempts to do so are likely to overstate mineralisation continuity , particularly for zones of 
higher grades.

14.9 GRADE ESTIMATION 
14.9.1 GOLD ESTIMATES 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project used a combination of ordinary kriging (OK) and localised uniform conditioning 
(LUC) estimation methods to interpolate gold grades into the block model. Hard boundaries were used within 
each of the overall mineralisation domains. 
A prerequisite for a LUC estimate is to first perform standard uniform conditioning (UC). This is achieved by 
running an OK estimate on a large block size termed the ‘panel’ (10 mE × 20 mN × 20 mRL), and then applying 
a ‘change of support’ correction based on the composite sample distribution and variogram model, 
conditioned to this panel grade estimate, to predict the likely grade tonnage distribution at the selective 
mining unit (SMU, being 5 mE × 10 mN × 10 mRL) within each panel. 
LUC requires initially that local ‘ranking’ (i.e. highest to lowest grade) of the SMU blocks is available with OK 
used to generate the SMU ranking within each panel. A quantile-quantile type matching of the SMU grade 
distribution, as determined by UC, with the ranked SMUs is then made. This yields the LUC SMU-scale grade 
estimates, which conform exactly to the SMU grade distribution predicted by the UC in panels. 
The LUC estimate was performed by Cube Consulting Pty Ltd (Cube) using Geovariances Isatis software. The 
flagged composite data, variogram parameters, search details and coded block model with mineralisation 
domains and dynamic anisotropy directions were prepared by Perseus and provided to Cube to complete 
the interpolation. 
Oriented search ellipsoids were used to define the local input data for estimation at each block. Search 
ellipsoid dimensions and anisotropy were based on orientations derived from semi-variogram analysis. Both 
the Nyanzaga and Kilimani mineralisation domains employed dynamic anisotropy, aligning the rotation of 
the search ellipsoid to the local dip and dip direction of the mineralis ation for each block. Estimation and 
search parameters for each area are provided in Table 14-13.

Validation of the estimates for the Nyanzaga Gold Project were completed using various methods.

grades, on a domain-by-domain basis.

composite grades (by easting, northing and RL), to the block model estimate grades for each domain.

14.11 CLASSIFICATION OF MINERAL RESOURCES 
Classification of the Nyanzaga Gold Project M ineral Resource was completed with consideration of the 
following criteria. 
• Resource drilling – the confidence in the interpretation boundaries and related mineralisation volumes 
related to the number, spacing, and orientation of the available drilling. 
• Continuity modelling – the spatial continuity of respective domains based on variogram analysis. 
• Estimation quality – the assessment of key estimation output statistics including slope of regression and 
average distance to samples.

236 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
• Validation results – the consideration of how well the underlying domain data is reflected in the 
estimated blocks as assessed by statistics globally and trend plots locally. 
A series of polygons were developed for the assignment of the applicable resource classification. In general, 
the classification criteria applied can be summarised as follows: 
• Indicated Resources 
• Areas with broadly regular drilling approximating 40 metre centres with average distance to samples 
generally less than 25 metres. 
• Domains defined by sufficient numbers of holes along strike and down dip to infer a suitable level of 
geological continuity. 
• Maximum extrapolation outside of drilling area of approximately 40 metres. 
• Inferred Resources 
• Areas with sufficient drilling to infer continuity along strike and down dip as supported by geology. 
• Maximum extrapolation of 80 metres. 
• Unclassified 
• Mineralised domains not otherwise classified. 
This general classification approach was adjusted to ensure consistent zones of equivalent classified 
resources were generated. The distribution of average sample distances by classification is presented in

15.3.2 MINERAL RESERVE DILUTION AND ORE LOSS 
In any mining operation, a degree of ore loss and dilution can be expected. This has the effect of altering the 
ore tonnages and grades predicted in the geological model. Factors influencing ore loss and dilution include 
deposit geometry, mining method, mining equipment size, mining practices and grade control processes. 
Based on the size and selectivity of the proposed mining equipment, the block size in the resource model 
(5.0 mE × 10.0 mN × 5.0 mRL) was considered suitable for the mining model and no re-blocking was required, 
with no additional ore loss or dilution applied. 
15.3.3 MINERAL RESERVE MODIFYING FACTORS 
15.3.3.1 MINING LEASE AND PHYSICAL MINING CONSTRAINTS 
Physical constraints are typically surface features that limit the allowable extent of mining. Examples include 
critical infrastructure, mining titles, property ownership and environmentally sensitive areas. 
The current exploitation permit covers a sufficient surface extent and does not constrain the mining or 
dumping limits. An allowance has been made for a 200 m buffer zone, inside the lease boundary, in which 
no mining activities will take place.  
Existing homes that fall within the mining lease will be rebuilt outside the lease in a location agreed on by 
both parties. An estimate of costs required for housing relocation and diversion of a perimeter road to 
outside of the lease boundary have been included in Perseus cost estimates. 
No geological constraints were applied to the pit optimisation, with Measured and Indicated Mineral 
Resources used to determine the pit limits. 
15.3.3.2 GEOLOGICAL BLOCK MODEL AND TOPOGRAPHY 
Mineral Resource models used for the estimation of Mineral Reserves provide material classifications based 
upon rock type (chert, mudstone, sandstone, upper volcanoclastic, lower volcanoclastic) and weathering 
surface (oxide, transitional or fresh). Different pit slopes, production rates, mining costs, processing 
parameters (throughputs, costs and recoveries) are applied to open pit Mineral Reserves at Nyanzaga, based 
upon different material types. These varying cost and rates are based upon feasibility level test work and 
studies. 
15.3.3.3 GEOTECHNICAL PARAMETERS 
Initial geotechnical investigation for the Nyanzaga deposit was completed during 2011 and 2012 by Golder 
Associates (Golder Associates, 2012). The program included geotechnical rock mass and structure data 
collection from 14 dedicated inclined diamond drill holes through the Nyanzaga (Tusker) deposit. Field and 
laboratory tests were completed on select diamond core samples and included point load, unconfined

241 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
compressive stress (UCS) and triaxial compressive stress tests to characterise the mechanical properties of 
the rock mass in line with the major geological unit and weathering subdivisions developed as part of the 
geology model. Using the same dataset, a geotechnical PFS study was undertaken by Mining Plus  that 
evaluated the project based on a combined mining method incorporating both open pit and underground 
mining (Mining Plus, 2016). 
An additional geotechnical drilling program to support a Feasibility Study for the previously proposed open 
pit and underground mine was completed in 2017, which was based  on a proposed drilling program by  
Mining Plus, with support from Peter O’Bryan & Associates (Mining Plus, 2016). The program included ten 
diamond drillholes targeting the underground mine design, supporting mine infrastructure, and sub-surface 
investigation to support the proposed box cut. A laboratory testing program was also completed, which 
consisted of UCS tests with elastic property determinations, direct shear tests of defects (bedding, joints, 
etc.) and acoustic emissions tests to estimate the in-situ stress regime. The tests were performed at Curtin 
University’s Western Australian School of Mines (WASM) in Kalgoorlie, Western Australia  (Western 
Australian School of Mines, 2018). 
The combined dataset of 24 geotechnical drillholes were supported by geotechnical logging of additional 
resource diamond drillholes to complete a geotechnical Feasibility Study for the combined open pit and 
underground mining option in 2022 by Peter O’Bryan and Associates (2022). 
The investigation programs included geotechnical rock mass and structural logging of the diamond core to 
classify the rock mass using industry standard classifications techniques, including rock mass rating (RMR), 
mining rock mass rating (MRMR) and the Q-system dependent on the mining method being evaluated. This 
information was used to provide a set of recommendations for appropriate slope angles for an open pit mine, 
and for inputs into underground mine design (for example, to provide recommended stope dimensions). 
Following completion of the acquisition by Perseus, the deposit has been further evaluated for a large stand-
alone open pit mine through a geotechnical assessment undertaken by MineGeoTech (MGT) in 2024  
(MineGeoTech, 2025). The geological model and weathering profile largely remained unchanged from the 
OreCorp DFS. The assessment focused on review of existing geotechnical data , but  also included the 
following additional items: 
• Manual relogging of drill core from the 2011-2012 and 2017  geotechnical programs for structural 
measurements in the fresh rock, excluding NYZGT005, NYZGT006, NYZGT012, NYZGT013, NYZGT018, 
NYZGT020 and NYZGT021. 
• Assessment and inclusion of geotechnical logs from diamond holes NYZDD1329 and NYZDD1330 from 
the 2024 resource drilling program. 
• Additional sampling and test work from existing fresh rock diamond drill core selected during the 2024 
relogging campaign. 
Manual relogging was undertaken on available drill holes to validate structural measurements and to rectify 
an identified systematic error in the measurement of structures recorded in the 2017 geotechnical program. 
This also allowed additional sample collection in the fresh rock units, as noted above. Sample intervals were 
selected to allow multiple labs to evaluate  the mechanical properties of similar geotechnical domains. A 
batch of samples was transported for Hoek triaxial and Brazilian indirect tensile strength testing at E Precision 
laboratory in Perth, Western Australia. Smaller batches were sent to in -country laboratories to conduct 
similar testing for evaluation and validation of results across the program. The evaluation program is ongoing. 
The geotechnical assessment by MGT classified the rock mass based on the main geological units and 
weathering sub-divisions for oxide, transitional and fresh rock. Structural kinematic analysis was used to 
assist the design of the slopes in the transitional and fresh sub -groups where structure orientation and 
interaction is expected to govern the design of appropriate batter and berm configurations. 
A high-level kinematic review of the various faults in the model was completed to assess potential for large-
scale interaction with the slope design. This review did not flag any significant foreseeable issues based on 
the modelled fault interpretations. Initial review of the modelled intersections of these structures against

16. MINING METHODS  
The Nyanzaga Gold Project is proposed to be mined by open pit mining methods. Such mining methods are 
well established in Tanzania, and across other African operations of Perseus Mining Limited. This Section 
outlines the key parameters and assumptions for mining of the Nyanzaga Mineral Reserve. 
16.1 OPEN PIT 
16.1.1 INTRODUCTION 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project open pits will use a conventional hydraulic excavator and rigid off-highway rear 
dump truck fleet, with drill and blast where required in oxide (38% blasted), transitional and fresh rock 
material. Mining bench heights are 10 m with 2.5 m flitches for selective mining to minimise ore loss and 
waste rock dilution. Bulk waste mining is also completed on 10 m benches. 
Open pit mining will be undertaken with medium to large scale off-highway equipment, including 
180 t – 350 t class excavators and 90 t – 150 t class dump trucks. Trucks haul ore to surface ore stockpiles, 
with waste being hauled to, and disposed in, waste rock dumps. Stockpile rehandle is by front-end loader. 
Drill and blast practices are employed to break competent rock. Drill and blast techniques, including pre-split 
and trim shots, are applied to minimise open pit wall damage, and blasting is configured to minimise ore loss 
and waste dilution.

16.1.3 MINING METHOD 
A conventional open pit mining method using excavators and rigid dump trucks was selected as the preferred 
mining method. Experienced mining contractors will undertake all aspects of the mining operation. 
Supervision, grade control and planning will be undertaken by an owner’s team. All fresh material will be 
blasted. Bulk waste will be blasted on 10 m benches and the ore zones will be blasted on 5 m benches and 
mined in two flitches for greater selectivity (depending on the point in the mine schedule) with ore delivered 
to blend fingers on the ROM pad. 
Mining activities are by a mining contractor, whose activities include stripping free dig material such as 
topsoil, clays and highly weathered rock near surface. Some oxide, transitional and fresh rock, which is the 
dominant material type, requires drilling and blasting, before being mined by the mining contractor. 
To balance waste stripping and ore grades, the pits are mined to the ultimate boundary limit using cutbacks. 
Access to the pit is by 26 m wide haul roads and ramps, incorporating a 10% gradient, with windrows and 
drains. Twin dual lane ramps are incorporated from the surface to 160 m from the base of the Pit. One dual 
lane ramp is incorporated from 160 m to 60 m to the base of the pit and single lane ramps, 16 m wide, are 
included for the final 60 m of the pit, as required towards the end of pit life to maximise ore recovery and 
minimise waste mining. Rock is hauled to the surface, with ore either direct tipped to the primary crusher or 
placed on stockpiles at the ROM pad, and waste dumped to waste rock dumps. 
Ore and waste in some of the oxide and all of the transition and fresh rock is drilled and blasted prior to 
excavation. The mine undertakes conventional drilling and blasting activities with pre-splitting in all transition 
and fresh rock to ensure stable wall conditions. 
16.1.4 MINING SCHEDULE 
The mining schedule for Nyanzaga is shown in Figure 16-5 and extends for 10 years , with total material 
movement forecast to peak during the period FY28 to FY32. The open pit mining operation has a current 
mining rate of approximately 50 Mt/a total material movement, and across the LOM, to deliver ore feed to 
support the target average processing rate of 5.5  Mt/a. Over the life of the open pit, 52.0  Mt of ore and 
297.8 Mt of waste will be mined at an average strip ratio of 5.7. 
A key constrain t with respect to mining at Nyanzaga is the vertical advance rate, which is limited to a
