17. RECOVERY METHODS  
17.1 INTRODUCTION 
The Nyanzaga gold processing plant has been designed by Lycopodium Minerals Pty Ltd with a nameplate 
ore treatment rate of 5.0 Mt/a (based on the projected ore blend with the highest weighted 85th percentile 
specific energy values) (Orway Mineral Consultants, 2024). Perseus notes the optionality to run at higher 
throughput rates based on ore specific comminution parameters, and major equipment selection and 
engineering has considered achieving higher volumetric throughput. 
This section summarises key technical data for the recovery of gold from Nyanzaga Gold Project ore types 
within the Nyanzaga processing plant facility. Section 17.3 summarises the development of design criteria 
for the Nyanzaga processing plant, based on findings from metallurgical test  work, circuit modelling and 
design engineering. Section 17.4 presents a simplified version of the Nyanzaga processing plant flowsheet 
and highlights major equipment specifications. Section 17.5 describes the gold recovery process and the 
process flowsheet in greater detail by plant area. Sections  17.7 and 17.8 summarise power and water 
requirements for processing Nyanzaga Gold Project ore deposits. 
17.2 SITE LOCATION AND LAYOUT 
The plant layout was developed based on an appropriate level of engineering effort required to support a 
Feasibility Study level capital cost estimate. The plant has been located to suit the available usable area within 
a restrictive topography, whilst providing appropriate access for all supporting infrastructure including 
mining, power supply and tailings storage. Due consideration for the interaction of these activities is critical 
for the effective operation of the processing plant and is captured in the overall site and plant layout. 
The design approach adopted reflects typical industry good practice, which will be continued and further 
developed during the detailed engineering of the Project. The Feasibility Study design incorporates 
Lycopodium’s extensive experience in gold plant design and project implementation in Africa. As the site and 
plant layout is aligned to the approach used for other African gold projects executed by Lycopodium Minerals 
Pty Ltd, the capital cost estimate presented in Section  21.1 inherently represents the cost of gold plant 
designs operated by international mining companies and designed to Australian standards. 
As shown in Figure 17-1, project facilities, including the mine services area, administration and  the 
accommodation village, have been located within close proximity of the process plant site  to maintain a 
single centre of operations. The plant area will be surrounded by a double security fence provided with 
perimeter lighting and camera monitoring. The plant layout provides ease of access to all equipment for 
operating and maintenance requirements while maintaining a compact footprint to minimise construction 
costs. All fixed plant and infrastructure facilities are located outside the 500 m blast radius of a conceptual 
$3,000/oz pit shell. 
A geotechnical investigation was conducted by Knight Piésold Pty Ltd during 2024 (Knight Piésold, 2025e) to 
confirm the location of the process plant and provide necessary information for process plant earthworks, 
concrete and structural design. Geotechnical investigations included test pits, borehole drilling, field testing, 
sampling and laboratory testing for key locations with major static and dynamic equipment loads. 
The typical sub-surface ground profile, based on logged ground conditions from the site investigation, is as 
follows: 
• Topsoil, comprising soft to firm sandy clay; soft to very stiff sandy and clayey silt; loose to medium dense 
silty and clayey sand; and medium dense to dense sandy gravel, with depths ranging from 0.3 m to 1.5 m. 
• Colluvium, comprising stiff to very stiff gravelly and sandy clay; dense to very dense gravelly sand; and 
medium dense to very dense sandy and clayey gravel, to depths ranging from 7.5 m to 12.95 m. 
• Residual soil, comprising stiff to hard gravelly and sandy clay; dense to very dense clayey and sandy 
gravel; loose to very dense clayey sand; and very stiff to hard clayey silt, to depths ranging from 7.5 m to 
40 m.

17.3 DESIGN CRITERIA DEVELOPMENT 
The mineral processing and metallurgical testing programs, detailed in Section 13, have provided information 
about the physical characteristics and metallurgical response of the Nyanzaga Gold Project ore deposits and 
ore types. Test work outcomes, along with typical industry design parameters, preliminary vendor data, 
Perseus instruction and Lycopodium experience have informed the process and engineering design criteria. 
The key criteria for equipment selection are the suitability for duty and the projected mine life of the 
operation without unnecessarily compromising reliability and ease of maintenance. 
The Nyanzaga plant will process a range of ore types ( predominantly oxide and fresh) with variable ore 
characteristics and head grades. The relative contributions of each material type and their proposed 
sequence of treatment over the LOM were considered during the sizing of the comminution circuit and 
subsequent modelling of plant throughput parameters. Predicted ore blend grades for both gold and silver 
have been considered  when sizing the CIL and  elution circuits and gold  room. The presence of low 
concentrations of soluble mercury have also been considered, and mercury treatment circuits have been 
included in the process flowsheet. 
The plant feed for the Nyanzaga Gold Project will consist of about 11.7% oxide and 88.3% fresh ore, with the 
majority of oxide ore processed in the first two years. The three main fresh ore lithologies are mudstone, 
sandstone and chert, with the more competent mudstone and sandstone ores making up the majority of the 
plant feed from year 2 onwards. The ore types, and their proportion of the LOM blend based on the plant 
feed schedule developed by Perseus, are shown in Table 17-1.

An SAB comminution circuit ( SAG milling with pebble recycle and ball milling in closed circuit with 
hydrocyclones) was selected for the Nyanzaga processing plant and will be  able to accommodate the 
spectrum of material hardness and competency observed from test work (Orway Mineral Consultants, 2024). 
Grind sensitivity and subsequent variability test work suggests that all material types are grind sensitive with 
gold extraction increasing with fineness of grind. The techno -economic grind optimisation evaluations 
identified that a grind size P80 of 75 μm is optimal for Nyanzaga Gold Project ores. Diagnostic leach test work 
and mineralogical investigations indicate that most of the residual gold that is not recoverable by cyanide at 
the target grind size is fine grained and associated with predominantly arsenopyrite, pyrite, pyrrhotite, 
carbonates, or silicates. Even though additional gold may be liberated with finer grinding, the incremental 
quantity of gold that would be liberated does not justify the incremental cost. 
Test work programs indicated that the gravity recovery stage added marginal benefit to the final gold 
extraction for most ore types. A gravity circuit has been included in the Nyanzaga process plant flowsheet 
for the following reasons: 
• Variable head assays for samples indicate that coarse gold or spotty mineralisation is present across 
Nyanzaga Gold Project ore deposits and ore types. This is best mitigated by inclusion of a gravity circuit, 
whereby potential spikes of high-grade material presenting to the CIL circuit are limited, allowing more 
consistent operation of the adsorption and elution circuits. 
• Leach kinetics are improved, particularly at the start of the leach, by removing the gravity recoverable 
gold. This improves the carbon profile and promotes lower gold solution losses.

255 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
• Intensive cyanidation of the gravity concentrate has improved potential of leaching gold from semi-
refractory minerals that may be present. 
• Removing gravity recoverable gold in a dedicated circuit reduces the amount of coarse gold that may 
accumulate in gravity traps across the comminution circuit, improving gold accountability and security 
outcomes. 
• Marginally reduced consumption of cyanide and lime were noted from test work. 
 
Gravity/cyanidation variability test work on Nyanzaga Gold Project  ore samples at optimised flowsheet 
conditions determined that average gold extractions by ore type ranged between 82.3% and 96.1%, and 
average silver extractions by ore type ranged between 26.5% and 66.1%. Gold leach kinetics were rapid, with 
most gold leaching occurring within four to eight hours. Silver leach kinetics were slower, with silver leaching 
being largely complete within 12  h, but continuing through to 24  h for some samples . Some mudstone 
samples exhibited mild preg -robbing characteristics, but these were demonstrated to be overcome by 
utilising a CIL circuit design . Mineralogical test work and multi element head assays across all ore types 
indicated that some samples contained elevated levels of sulfide minerals (e.g., pyrite, pyrrhotite , 
arsenopyrite), which increase oxygen demand in cyanide leach. Consequently, the plant design comprises a 
single pre-oxidation stage ahead of a six -stage CIL circuit. Oxygen addition was shown to promote leach 
kinetics across test work programs, so the pre-oxidation and CIL tanks will be fitted with oxygen addition 
down shaft of agitators. The CIL circuit has been designed to have a nameplate residence time of 24 h. 
Oxide ore samples tested in rheology, thickening and settling rate tests exhibited performance limitations 
once 60% w/w solids is reached, whereas fresh ore samples did not exhibit performance limitations up to 
the maximum pulp density tested at 60% w/w solids. Pre-leach and tailings thickeners have been included in 
the Nyanzaga Gold Project flowsheet to maximum water recycle, with CIL design pulp density of 50% w/w 
solids selected and supported by test work. 
It was noted that the Nyanzaga and Kilimani deposit ores contain elevated concentrations of mercury, arsenic 
and antimony. The ore processing flowsheet has been designed to capture mercury through a range of 
mercury abatement technologies, described in Section  17.5.12. Test work and modelling indicates that 
soluble arsenic and soluble antimony will not have a significant effect on potential economic recovery of gold 
in CIL and that soluble arsenic and soluble antimony will be contained within the tailings and process water 
systems. Provision has been made in sustaining capital for a water treatment plant should arsenic or 
antimony present operational challenges in the future. pH control is included in the process control design 
to mitigate gold passivation that can occur at high pH due to elevated antimony levels. 
Cyanide detoxification of the tails stream is included in the Nyanzaga plant flowsheet to ensure that TSF 
supernatant concentrations achieve CNWAD levels <50 mg/L, which aligns with industry guidelines for TSFs 
such as Standard of Practice 4.4 of  International Cyanide Management Institute’s Mining Operations 
Verification Protocol (2021).

17.4 PROCESS FLOWSHEET 
The process plant design for the Nyanzaga Gold Project is based on a robust metallurgical flowsheet designed 
for optimum recovery with minimal operating costs. The flowsheet is based on unit operations that are well 
proven in industry. A simplified process flow diagram for the Nyanzaga process plant is shown in Figure 17-2, 
and consists of the following unit processes: 
• Primary crushing with a single gyratory crusher to produce a coarse crushed product. 
• A live stockpile from which ore is reclaimed to feed the milling circuit. 
• SAG milling with pebble recycle and ball milling in closed circuit with hydrocyclones (SAB comminution) 
to produce a grind size of 80% passing (P80) of 75 µm. 
• Gravity concentration and removal of coarse gold from the circulating load within the milling circuit, and 
treatment of gravity concentrate by intensive cyanidation and electrowinning. 
• Trash screening of the cyclone overflow stream, to remove wood and plastic trash or oversize material 
prior to cyanidation. 
• Pre-leach thickening of the trash screen underflow to increase the slurry density feeding the carbon-in-
leach (CIL) circuit and optimise water recycle within the process. 
• A pre-oxidation/CIL circuit to leach and adsorb gold and silver from the milled ore onto activated carbon. 
This circuit consists of one pre-oxidation tank, and six CIL tanks, providing a total of 24 hours leach and 
adsorption time. 
• A split AARL elution circuit for recovery of precious metals from loaded CIL carbon. 
• Electrowinning.

• Carbon regeneration. 
• Smelting of electrowinning sludge, producing doré for sale. 
• Mercury recovery from electrowinning sludge, and electrowinning cell, smelting furnace and carbon 
reactivation kiln off gases. 
• Thickening of CIL tailings to produce a higher solids concentration slurry for tailings storage facility (TSF) 
deposition and optimise water recycle within the process. 
• SO2/air detoxification of cyanide in tailings thickener underflow slurry. 
• Pumping of cyanide detoxification tailings to the TSF. 
• Return of TSF decant water for process use.

17.5 PROCESS AND PLANT DESCRIPTION 
17.5.1 CONTROL SYSTEM 
17.5.1.1 GENERAL 
The general control philosophy for the plant will be one with a high level of automation and remote control 
facilities. Instrumentation will be provided within the plant to measure and control key process parameters. 
The main control room will house two PC based operator interface terminals (OIT). Two additional servers 
will also be located here to act as the control system supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) servers 
in a redundant configuration. The control room is intended to provide a central area from where the plant is 
operated and monitored and from which the regulatory control loops can be monitored and adjusted. All 
key process and maintenance parameters will be available for trending and alarming on the process control

260 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
system (PCS). An additional OIT will be located at the top of the crusher building , to provide a  secondary 
location for crushing circuit monitoring and control. 
The PCS that will be used for the plant will be a programmable logic controller (PLC) and SCADA based system. 
The PCS will control the process interlocks and PID (proportional-integral-derivative) control loops for non-
packaged equipment. 
Vendor supplied packages will use vendor standard control systems throughout the project. Vendor packages 
will generally have limited interfaces with the PCS such that control and set-point changes may have to be 
adjusted locally. General equipment fault alarms from each vendor package will be monitored by the PCS 
system and displayed on the OIT. Fault diagnostics and troubleshooting of vendor packages will be performed 
locally. 
17.5.1.2 FIELD INPUT / OUTPUT 
All instrumentation and field controls will be captured by the PCS via remote input/output (I/O) modules, 
generally located at each process module of the plant, primarily to minimise extended cable run lengths back 
to the switchroom. These remote I/O modules are electrical field enclosures housing power supplies, 
network equipment, marshalling terminals and PLC remote I/O nodes. All remote I/O nodes will be linked to 
the PLC via a PCS Ethernet network, supported over the site fibre optic cabling between switchrooms, remote 
I/O modules and key infrastructure buildings. 
17.5.1.3 DRIVE CONTROL 
In general, the plant process drives will report their ready, run and start push button status to the PCS and 
will be displayed on the OIT. Local control stations will be in the field in proximity to the relevant drives. These 
will, as a minimum, contain start and latch-off-stop (LOS) pushbuttons which will be hard-wired to the drive 
starter. Plant drives will predominantly be started by the control system in automatic operation. 
The OITs will allow drives to be selected to Auto, Local, Remote or Out-of-Service modes via the drive control 
pop up. Statutory interlocks, such as emergency stops and thermal protection, will be hardwired and will 
apply in all modes of operation. All PLC generated process interlocks will apply in Auto and Remote modes. 
Process interlocks will be disabled or bypassed in Local mode, except for critical interlocks such as lubrication 
systems on grinding mills. 
Local selection will allow each drive to be operated by the operator in the field via the local start push button. 
Remote selection will allow the equipment to be started from the control room via the drive control pop up. 
Status indication of process interlocks, as well as the selected mode of operation, will be displayed on the 
OIT. 
17.5.1.4 CONTROL LOOPS 
Regulatory control loops will be provided for all key process circuits to provide optimal functionality without 
regular operator intervention. 
There will be two modes for loop-controlled set points available in the OIT. These are 'Loop Auto Mode' and 
'Loop Manual Mode'. In Loop Auto Mode (analogous to cascade control), the set point will be predominantly 
controlled by the applicable master PID loop (e.g., for thickener underflow pumping control, the bed pressure 
PID controller output will supply a set point for the thickener underflow flow control loop, which ultimately 
controls the speed of the thickener underflow pump). In Loop Manual Mode, set point may be entered 
manually from the loop set point pop up in the OIT. 
Where required, analogue set points from the PCS to vendor supplied control panels can be done either via 
the OIT or via vendor control panels. 
17.5.2 ROM PAD 
The run-of-mine (ROM) pad is used to provide a buffer between the mine and the plant. ROM stockpiles 
allow blending of ore types and grades to ensure a consistent feed type and feed rate to the plant.

261 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
Mining haul trucks operating from the open pit mine will deliver run-of-mine (ROM) ore to the ROM pad, 
where it will be direct tipped to the ROM bin or dumped to blending stockpiles. A front-end loader (FEL) will 
be used to reclaim ore from the various ROM pad stockpiles to the ROM bin. 
The ROM bin will be equipped with raw water sprays to provide dust suppression whilst ore is fed to the 
ROM bin. 
17.5.3 CRUSHING CIRCUIT 
ROM ore will be loaded into the ROM bin by direct tipping from mining haul trucks or reclaimed by FEL from 
the ROM pad stockpiles. A mobile rock breaker will be utilised to break oversize rocks on the ROM pad, whilst 
a fixed rock breaker will be utilised to break oversize rocks that report to the ROM bin. 
Ore that is delivered to the ROM bin will report to the primary gyratory crusher. Crusher product will be 
drawn from the primary crusher discharge bin by the crusher discharge conveyor. The crusher discharge 
conveyor will transfer onto the stockpile feed conveyor. A weightometer located near the discharge end of 
the crusher discharge conveyor will indicate the instantaneous and totalised crushing circuit tonnage. 
A dust collector will be installed to capture dust from material transfer points within the crushing circuit. 
The crushing circuit will be primarily monitored and controlled from the plant control room, with secondary 
monitoring and control available from an OIT located at the upper level of the primary crusher . Two-way 
radio communication between the control room operator and the ROM pad vehicles will ensure that a 
minimum inventory is maintained within the ROM bin. 
17.5.4 COARSE ORE STOCKPILE AND RECLAIM 
The stockpile feed conveyor will discharge crushed ore onto the coarse ore stockpile (COS). The COS has a 
live capacity of 14.5 h and is supplemented by a further approximately three days’ worth of ore that is side 
cast and can be reclaimed by FEL. Raw water sprays will be installed for dust suppression as required. 
Crushed ore will be reclaimed from the COS at a controlled rate by the variable speed stockpile reclaim 
feeders, which will discharge onto the stockpile reclaim conveyor. The crushed ore will then be transferred 
to the grinding circuit via the SAG mill feed conveyor. Crushed ore can also be reclaimed by FEL from the COS 
into the emergency reclaim feeder bin. The variable speed emergency reclaim feeder will withdraw and 
transfer ore from the emergency reclaim feeder bin to the emergency reclaim conveyor and then to the SAG 
mill feed conveyor. A weightometer beneath the SAG mill feed conveyor will indicate the instantaneous and 
totalised mill feed tonnage and will be used to control the speed of the stockpile reclaim feeders or the 
emergency reclaim feeder. 
The reclaim circuit will be controlled from the plant control room. 
17.5.5 GRINDING AND CLASSIFICATION CIRCUIT 
Crushed ore will be milled to achieve the required grind size for effective gold recovery by cyanidation. The 
grinding circuit will consist of a SAG mill with pebble recycle and a ball mill in closed circuit with a cluster of 
hydrocyclones (SAB comminution circuit). 
Ore feeding the SAG mill is slurrified with mill water and subjected to primary grinding in the presence of 
SAG mill grinding media. The SAG mill will be equipped with a variable speed drive to assist in managing 
variations in ore competency and  hardness. Slurry discharging from the SAG mill will feed to a pebble 
dewatering screen. The oversize, consisting of pebbles and worn steel grinding media, will discharge onto 
the pebble transfer conveyor and will then be transferred to the SAG mill feed conveyor via the pebble 
discharge conveyor. If required, pebble dewatering screen oversize can be diverted to the milling area sump. 
A weightometer will be fitted beneath the pebble discharge conveyor to indicate the mass of pebbles being 
recycled. Should the competency and hardness of future ore sources increase , sufficient space has been 
allowed for retrofitting a pebble crushing circuit.

A jib crane will be provided for maintenance of the cyclones. Maintenance lifts around the mills will be done

and bolt removal tool will be provided for mill liner changeouts. 
17.5.6 GRAVITY CIRCUIT 
A dedicated gravity feed pump will pump mill discharge hopper slurry to the gravity circuit, which will consist 
of two gravity scalping screens and two centrifugal gravity concentrators. An intensive cyanidation reactor 
will process the gravity concentrate. 
Slurry feeding the gravity circuit will report to the gravity scalping screens, with screen oversize reporting to 
the mill discharge hopper. Undersize slurry from each screen will report to a centrifugal gravity concentrator 
beneath each screen. Each gravity concentrator will be  operated as a semi -batch process with periodic 
discharge of coarse, high SG material (gravity concentrate) to the feed hopper of the intensive cyanidation 
reactor. The tails slurry from the centrifugal gravity concentrators will gravitate to the mill discharge hopper. 
The intensive cyanidation reactor will process one batch of gravity concentrate per day  under intensive 
cyanidation conditions. Sodium cyanide, caustic soda and oxygen will be introduced into the slurry, with the 
leach cycle lasting for up to 20 h. Flocculant will be added at the end of the leach cycle to settle the leach 
solids. The pregnant solution will be separated from the solids and pumped to a dedicated gravity pregnant 
solution tank adjacent to the gold room. Intensive cyanidation tails will be pumped back to the mill discharge 
hopper for additional grinding to recover any remaining entrained gold. 
A dedicated water pump from the process water pond will provide filtered fluidisation water for the 
centrifugal concentrators, at the required constant pressure and flow. 
The centrifugal concentrators and intensive cyanidation reactor will be located in a separate building 
enclosed with secure mesh. 
17.5.7 TRASH SCREENING 
Milled slurry will gravitate from the cyclone cluster overflow to the trash screen feed box and will be fed to 
the vibrating trash screen.  The trash screen will remove any misreporting coarse ore particles, wood 
fragments and plastics that may adversely affect the performance of the CIL and elution circuits. 
Trash material will gravitate to the trash bunker and will be cleaned out periodically using a FEL. The trash 
bunker area will be bunded with a sump provided to pump any spillage to the tails hopper. 
Trash screen underflow slurry will gravitate to pre-leach thickening. 
17.5.8 LEACH FEED SAMPLING AND PRE-LEACH THICKENING 
Trash screen underflow  slurry will gravitate to the pre -leach thickening area , where the slurry will be 
thickened to the target pulp density for the leach circuit.

Flocculant will be diluted using a static mixer and mixed with the pre-leach thickener feed slurry in the pre-
leach thickener feed box to facilitate effective settling. The flocculant addition rate will be adjusted to control 
the bed level of the settled solids and clarity of the thickener overflow water. 
Pre-leach thickener underflow will be pumped by the leach feed pumps to a two-stage leach feed sampler, 
that will produce shift composite samples from incremental sample cuts at timed intervals. Sampler 
discharge will report to the leach feed distribution launder. If the thickener underflow density is too low or 
the downstream processes have stopped, the thickener will be put into recirculation mode with thickener 
underflow pumped to the pre-leach thickener feed box. 
Pre-leach thickener overflow will gravitate to the mill water tank for distribution as dilution water to the 
grinding circuit. Process water will be added to the mill water tank as required to make up the mill water 
requirements. 
The pre-leach thickening area sump pump will pump any spillage to the pre-leach thickener feed box or to 
the leach feed distribution launder. 
17.5.9 LEACH AND ADSORPTION CIRCUIT 
The leach and adsorption circuit will consist of one pre -oxidation and six CIL tanks, all with identical live 
volumes. The six leach tanks will provide a nameplate residence time of 24  h. The tanks will be 
interconnected with launders and slurry will flow by gravity through the tank train. Each tank will be fitted 
with an agitator to ensure that the slurry is thoroughly mixed  and homogenised. Each CIL tank will be 
equipped with a mechanically swept intertank screen to retain carbon within the tank, and a recessed 
impeller carbon transfer pump to facilitate carbon transfer between adjacent CIL tanks. All tanks will be fitted 
with bypass facilities to allow any tank to be removed from service. 
Pre-leach thickener underflow will be pumped by the leach feed pumps to the leach feed distribution launder 
via a two-stage leach feed sampler and then gravitate to the pre-oxidation tank. Oxygen gas will be sparged 
down the shaft of the pre-oxidation tank agitator to pre-treat leach feed slurry. This step will promote 
oxidation of sulfide minerals, such as pyrite, arsenopyrite and pyrrhotite. The oxidation of minerals in the 
pre-oxidation tank will allow for enhanced gold leaching, r educed consumption of sodium cyanide and 
improved gold recovery in the CIL tanks. 
After pre-oxidation, gold will be leached from the slurry  in the CIL tanks and recovered from the leach 
solution by adsorption onto activated carbon. Quicklime will be added to the SAG mill feed conveyor to 
ensure that the leach slurry pH is sufficiently elevated and suitable for cyanidation. Sodium cyanide solution 
will be metered into the CIL tanks. Oxygen gas will be sparged down the shafts of the CIL tank agitators to 
provide the required dissolved oxygen concentration for the leach reaction. 
Sodium cyanide can also dissolve deleterious elements that may occur in low concentrations in ore. In the 
case of Nyanzaga Gold Project ores subjected to metallurgical test work, it has been identified that mercury 
will also be leached in the CIL tanks. Any leached mercury will adsorb onto activated carbon along with gold. 
The recovery and handling of mercury is discussed further in Section 17.5.12. 
Regenerated barren carbon will be added to the final CIL tank (CIL tank 6) via the carbon sizing screen 
overflow and will be advanced counter-current to the slurry flow. Carbon will be advanced by pumping slurry 
and carbon from the downstream tank to the upstream tank. Any carbon will be retained in the upstream 
tank by the intertank screen whilst the slurry will flow by gravity back to the downstream tank. This counter-
current process will be repeated until the carbon eventually reaches the first CIL tank (CIL tank 1). 
Loaded carbon will be removed from the circuit by pumping CIL tank 1 slurry and carbon to the loaded carbon 
recovery screen. The loaded carbon will be washed on the screen to remove fine ore particles and will report 
as screen oversize to the acid wash column. The screen undersize slurry will gravitate back to CIL tank 1. 
Slurry from the last CIL tank will leave the CIL circuit and will gravitate to the CIL tails samplers and the carbon 
safety screen. 
Fine carbon and quench/transfer water is removed via the carbon sizing screen undersize stream.

A gantry crane mounted on rails on top of the train of pre-oxidation and CIL tanks will provide ready access 
for maintenance, particularly for intertank screen changeout and cleaning. 
Four CIL area sump pumps will pump any spillage back into the pre-oxidation/CIL circuit. 
17.5.10 ACID WASH, ELUTION AND CARBON REGENERATION  
The following operations will be carried out in the elution area: 
• Acid washing of loaded carbon. 
• Desorption of gold from loaded carbon using split AARL elution. 
• Regeneration of barren carbon. 
 
The elution area will be designed to treat one batch of carbon per day and a total of six batches of carbon 
per week, though back-to-back stripping can treat seven batches of carbon per week when required. The 
elution area will include an acid wash column, an elution column , a strip solution heater and a carbon 
regeneration kiln. 
Loaded carbon will be recovered from slurry in the first CIL tank via the loaded carbon recovery screen and 
reports to the acid wash column. The loaded carbon will be washed with a dilute hydrochloric acid solution 
to remove inorganic contaminants prior to being rinsed with water. Acid wash solution effluent reports to 
the tails hopper. 
Acid washed loaded carbon will be hydraulically transferred to the elution column where it will be eluted 
with a hot dilute cyanide/caustic solution followed by a hot water wash. The gold will be recovered from the 
carbon into pregnant solution that will report to one of the pregnant solution tanks located adjacent to the 
gold room. Mercury will also desorb from the carbon during the elution cycle and will report to the pregnant 
solution. 
After elution, the barren carbon will be hydraulically transferred to the carbon dewatering screen, where it 
will be dewatered before reporting to the horizontal rotating carbon regeneration kiln. The barren carbon 
will be heated to 750°C in an oxygen deficient and steam rich atmosphere to remove organic contaminants 
prior to being cooled in the carbon quench hopper. During the high temperature regeneration reaction, the 
portion of mercury remaining on barren carbon  will be vaporised, recovered and contained (see  
Section 17.5.12). The regenerated barren carbon will be hydraulically transferred back to the carbon sizing 
screen, where it will be dewatered before reporting to the last CIL tank. 
17.5.11 GOLD RECOVERY 
The following operations will be carried out in the gold room area: 
• Electrowinning of gold from gravity pregnant solution. 
• Electrowinning of gold from elution pregnant solution. 
• Smelting of electrowinning products. 
 
Pregnant solution, recovered from the gravity circuit, will be pumped from the gravity pregnant solution tank 
to the dedicated gravity electrowinning cell. Gold will be recovered onto stainless steel cathodes , and 
solution will be circulated back to the gravity pregnant solution tank. Recirculation of the pregnant solution 
through the gravity electrowinning cell will continue until the precious metal tenor is sufficiently depleted. 
Spent electrolyte will be recycled to the head of the CIL circuit. 
Pregnant solution, recovered from the elution circuit, will be pumped from one of the elution pregnant 
solution tanks to dedicated elution electrowinning cells. Gold will be recovered onto stainless steel cathodes, 
and solution will be circulated back to the elution pregnant solution tank. Recirculation of the pregnant

solution through the elution electrowinning cells will continue until the precious metal tenor is sufficiently 
depleted. Spent electrolyte will be recycled to the head of the CIL circuit. 
Cathodes from the gravity electrowinning cell will be treated separately from cathodes from the elution 
electrowinning cells to assist with metallurgical accounting. Gold will be removed from the cathodes by high 
pressure spray wash water, with the gold sludge being filtered and dried in the retort oven. As the sludge is 
drying, any contained mercury will be vaporised, recovered and contained (see Section 17.5.12). The dried 
sludge will be mixed with fluxes and smelted in a smelting furnace to produce doré bars. Slag from smelting 
operations will be returned to the milling circuit via the emergency reclaim feeder bin. 
Fume extraction equipment will be provided to remove electrowinning cell gases and off gas from the 
smelting furnace. Handling of these gases  is discussed further in Section  17.5.12. In addition to this, 
ventilation fans will be provided to ensure there is adequate fresh air recycling inside the gold room. 
An overhead crane within the gold room will be provided to assist with handling of electrowinning cell 
cathodes and anodes. 
The gold room area sump pump will pump any spillage from the electrowinning cells and sludge pan filter 
into the pre-oxidation/CIL circuit. 
17.5.12 MERCURY HANDLING 
Mercury, a deleterious element that can occur in low concentrations in Nyanzaga Gold Project ore, can be 
dissolved by sodium cyanide solution in CIL tanks and concentrate in process streams. As mercury is a health 
hazard, controls to limit exposure will be required. 
Mercury that may be dissolved by sodium cyanide in CIL tanks will adsorb onto activated carbon along with 
gold. Some mercury will desorb from loaded carbon during elution cycle s and will report to pregnant 
solution. Mercury contained in this stream will report to electrowinning cell sludge. The filtered 
electrowinning sludge will be dried in a retort oven so that any contained mercury is recovered safely. The 
mercury retort will be located within a separate room within the gold room, with the retort room maintained 
at negative pressure when the retort is operational to ensure mercury containment. The retort oven consists 
of the retort oven chamber, retort water chiller, retort condenser tube, retort collection tank, retort 
aftercooler condenser, retort oven aftercooler air filter, retort oven aftercooler carbon filters and retort 
vacuum pump. 
Filtered electrowinning sludge will be loaded onto the retort oven trays and placed inside the retort oven 
chamber. On heating, any water and mercury contained in the sludge will vaporise , with oven off -gases 
pulled from the chamber by the retort vacuum pump. The gases will pass through the retort condenser tube, 
where chilled water will be used to cool the gases and condense the water vapour and the majority of the 
mercury, which will gravitate to the retort collection tank. The cleaned off gases will pass through the retort 
aftercooler condenser, retort oven aftercooler air filter, and sulfur impregnated aftercooler carbon filters for 
residual mercury vapour removal prior to venting to atmosphere. At the end of each retort cycle, the mercury 
will be drained from the separator into a mercury storage flask and the water will be drained to the retort 
area sump and pumped to the tails hopper. 
The mercury transfer area will have a steel floor pan, allowing any spillage to be contained and recovered. 
The mercury storage flasks will be stored in the retort room until they are removed from site for downstream 
treatment by others. Sulfur impregnated carbon in the retort oven aftercooler carbon filters will be replaced 
with fresh carbon as required, with the mercury laden carbon placed into a drum and stored. 
Off gases and vapour will be drawn through fume ducting systems placed above electrowinning cells, the 
smelting furnace and the retort oven by fume fans. The off gases will pass through the gold room fume wet 
scrubber, where filtered water will be used to cool the gases and condense vapours, dust and mercury, which 
will gravitate to the gold room fume wet scrubber hopper. The cleaned off gases will be drawn through to 
the gold room carbon filter feed heater and then pass through the  sulfur impregnated gold room fume 
carbon filter  for residual mercury vapour removal prior to venting to atmosphere. Mercury will be 
periodically drained from the gold room fume wet scrubber hopper into a mercury storage flask and the

the gold room fume carbon filter will be replaced with fresh carbon as required, with the mercury laden

Mercury that is not desorbed from loaded carbon during elution cycles will report to barren carbon. During

17.5.13 TAILINGS SAMPLING, THICKENING, TREATMENT AND DISPOSAL 
CIL tailings will gravitate to a two-stage CIL tails sampler, that will produce shift composite samples from 
incremental sample cuts at timed intervals. Sampler discharge will report to the carbon safety screen, that 
will prevent coarse carbon from being lost to the TSF. Screen oversize (recovered carbon) will be collected in 
bags for subsequent return to the CIL circuit. The screen underflow will gravitate to the tailings thickening 
area, where the slurry will be thickened to the target pulp density for cyanide detoxification and tailings 
deposition. 
Flocculant will be diluted using a static mixer and mixed with the tailings thickener feed slurry in the tailings 
thickener feed box to facilitate effective settling. The flocculant addition rate will be adjusted to control the 
bed level of the settled solids and clarity of the thickener overflow water. Tailings thickener underflow will 
be pumped to the cyanide detoxification circuit by the cyanide detoxification feed pumps. If the thickener 
underflow density is too low or the downstream processes have stop ped, the thickener will be put into 
recirculation mode with thickener underflow pumped to the tailings thickener feed box. 
Tailings thickener overflow will gravitate to the process water tank for distribution primarily downstream of 
the grinding circuit. Raw water will be added to the process water tank as required to make up the process 
water requirements serviced by this tank. 
The tailings thickening area sump pump will pump any spillage to the tailings thickener feed box. 
The cyanide destruction circuit will consist of a feed distribution box and two cyanide detoxification tanks. 
Each tank will be fitted with an agitator to ensure that the slurry is thoroughly mixed and homogenised and 
oxygen gas will be sparged down the shaft of the cyanide detoxification tank agitators. Sodium metabisulfite 
(SMBS) and copper sulfate are added to the tanks, as required, to reduce the weak acid dissociable (WAD) 
cyanide concentration in solution below target values. Provision has been made for online WAD cyanide 
analysis to monitor the effectiveness of the cyanide detoxification  circuit on reducing the WAD cyanide  
concentration being discharged to the tailings storage facility (TSF). Both the cyanide detoxification feed and 
tailings streams will be sampled and measured for WAD cyanide concentration. 
Tailings slurry from the cyanide destruction circuit  will then report to the tails hopper, where it will be 
combined with various other process effluent streams. The final tailings slurry will then be pumped via the 
tails pumps to the TSF for disposal.

The cyanide detoxification and tails hopper area will have one sump pump to pump any spillage to either the 
tails hopper or the cyanide detoxification tanks. 
Tailings will be deposited sub-aerially into the TSF from the southern perimeter using multiple spigots. The

17.5.14 REAGENTS AND CONSUMABLES 
17.5.14.1 STORAGE 
Reagents will be received on site either in bulk or in shipping containers, with a 28 to 60 days’ worth of stock 
stored on site, depending on the reagent and source of supply. This will ensure that supply interruptions due 
to port, transport or weather delays do not restrict production. 
17.5.14.2 GRINDING MEDIA 
SAG and ball mill grinding media will be delivered to site either in bulk, in drums or in bulk bags. SAG mill 
grinding media will be reclaimed by FEL from the SAG mill ball bunker and loaded into the SAG mill ball 
charger. The SAG mill ball charger will periodically meter SAG mill grinding media onto the SAG mill feed 
conveyor. 
Ball mill grinding media will be reclaimed by FEL from the ball mill ball bunker and loaded into the ball mill 
ball charger. The ball mill ball charger discharges ball mill grinding media to fill the ball mill ball charging 
kibble, which is lifted and discharged into the ball mill feed box. 
Grinding media charging will be carried as required to maintain the target power draw in the SAG mill and 
ball mill. 
17.5.14.3 QUICKLIME 
Quicklime will be delivered to the site as a dry powder in bulk lime tankers and pneumatically transferred 
into the lime silo using a lime blower. The lime silo will be equipped with a reverse pulse bag filter, to minimise 
dust emissions during loading, and a bin activator. 
Quicklime will be metered from the lime silo via a variable speed rotary valve directly onto the SAG mill feed 
conveyor to achieve the desired pH downstream in the cyanide leach circuit. 
17.5.14.4 FLOCCULANT 
Flocculant will be delivered to site in bulk bags as a dry powder and will be added to the flocculant bag 
breaker. The vendor supplied flocculant mixing plant will automatically mix batches of flocculant with raw 
water and transfer the mixed flocculant to the flocculant storage tank after each mixing cycle is complete. 
Dedicated pumps will meter the flocculant solution to the pre-leach thickener and tailings thickener, where 
the flocculant solution will promote settling of solids and improve solid -water separation within the 
thickeners. 
Liquid flocculant will be delivered to site in 1,000 L intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) and pumped to the 
intensive cyanidation reactor as required using a dedicated dosing pump. 
17.5.14.5 CYANIDE 
Sodium cyanide (NaCN) will be delivered as dry briquettes in bulk bags. The cyanide bags will be lifted into 
the cyanide bag breaker above the agitated cyanide mixing tank and dissolved in process water to achieve

17.5.14.6 OXYGEN 
Pressure Swing Adsorption (PSA) oxygen plants will be installed to provide the oxygen requirements for gold

Activated carbon will be delivered in bulk bags and will be added via the carbon quench hopper to top up the 
inventory of activated carbon within the CIL circuit as required. This addition point will allow any fine carbon 
particles to be removed via the carbon sizing screen prior to entering the CIL circuit. Activated carbon will act 
as the adsorbent for precious metal species dissolved by cyanide in the CIL circuit. 
17.5.14.8 HYDROCHLORIC ACID 
Concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) will be delivered to site in intermediate bulk containers (IBCs). The 
concentrated hydrochloric acid will be pumped into the HCl acid mixing and storage tank where it will be 
diluted with filtered water to achieve the required acid wash solution concentration. The dilute acid solution 
will be pumped to the acid wash column to remove inorganic impurities from loaded carbon into an effluent 
solution stream. 
17.5.14.9 CAUSTIC SODA 
Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide, NaOH) will be delivered to site as dry pearl pellets in bulk bags. The caustic 
soda bags will be lifted into the caustic bag breaker above the agitated caustic mixing tank. The pellets will 
be metered into the caustic mixing tank via a screw feeder and dissolved in raw water to the required solution 
concentration. 
Caustic dosing pumps will meter the caustic soda solution, as required, to the intensive cyanidation reactor,

conductivity for electrowinning, and into the elution circuit for the desorption of gold from loaded carbon.

supernatant WAD cyanide solution concentrations below target levels.

17.5.15.5 FILTERED WATER 
Filtered water for the process plant will be produced by treating raw water in the filtered water treatment

17.5.15.7 FIRE WATER 
Fire water for the process plant and surrounding surface operations will be sourced from the raw water pond. 
The fire water suction from the raw water pond will be at a lower level than the raw water supply suction to 
ensure a fire water reserve always remains in the pond. 
The firewater pumping system will contain: 
• An electric fire water jockey pump to maintain fire water ring main pressure. 
• An electric fire water pump to supply fire water at the required pressure and flow rate.

17.8 WATER REQUIREMENTS 
The Nyanzaga processing plant will use water sourced from Lake Victoria or recycled water. Water will be 
recycled from the TSF supernatant pond via the TSF decant, as well as from pre-leach thickener overflow and 
tailings thickener overflow. Water that is in excess of operating requirements within mining operations (from 
pit runoff or open pit dewatering) may also be directed to the process water pond. The processing plant 
water services are described in further detail in Section 17.5.15. 
Mass balance modelling (Lycopodium, 2025a), (Knight Piésold, 2025a) indicates that raw water abstraction 
requirements from Lake Victoria will range from 50 m3/h to 350 m3/h once TSF decant return water flow has 
been established , which is equivalent to between 0. 08 m3/t and 0.56 m3/t ore treated. In the first 
approximately five months of operation, before TSF decant return water flow has been established, raw 
water abstraction requirements from Lake Victoria will be approximately 550 m3/h (equivalent of 0.88 m3/t 
ore treated). 
In consideration of variable water demands by ore type, variable ore treatment rates by ore type, downtime 
required for pump and pipeline maintenance, and design margin, installed lake abstraction pumping capacity 
will be 600 m3/h. 
Within the process plant, the process water pond will have an installed capacity of 18,000 m3 and the raw 
water pond will have an installed capacity of 10,000 m3.

18.6.1 GRID POWER SUPPLY

The Nyanzaga substation will contain two duty 220/11  kV 25/33 MVA transformers, with one spare only

18.6.2 POWER QUALITY CONSIDERATIONS 
Poor power quality in the north of Tanzania has historically been an issue as a result of the high concentration 
of power generation in the south of the country and the large loads (including those associated with the 
mining industry) in the north. There have been significant efforts undertaken by TANESCO to strengthen the

285 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
supply in the north, including a 220 kV fixed series compensator (FSC) at Dodoma, a 220 kV static VAR (volt-
ampere reactive) compensator (SVC) at Shinyanga, and some shunt capacitor installations. 
One of the projects that has been completed is the implementation of a 400 kV double circuit twin bundle 
BlueJay conductor transmission line and substation upgrades between Iringa and Shinyanga – significantly 
strengthening the power system in the north of the country. With the improvements in the grid stability, the 
reliability and power quality of the supply is vastly improved and is now suitable to meet the requirements 
of the site total mining load. 
18.6.3 POWER FACTOR CORRECTION 
Power factor correction is necessary to meet the minimum power factor requirement of 0.95 lagging for a 
grid connected load. High voltage power factor correction units will be installed at the Site 11 kV switchboard 
to control the power factor at the incomer supply to the main plant 11 kV switchboard. 
18.6.4 NYANZAGA SUBSTATION 
The receiving end substation at Nyanzaga will consist of two 25/33 MVA ONAN/ONAF transformers to step 
down the voltage from 220 kV to the 11 kV site distribution voltage. A third spare transformer will be installed 
in the switchyard; however, this will only be energised at 11 kV and is a spare only. The transformers will 
connect to an 11  kV switchboard to be located adjacent to the substation. The plant switchboard will be 
directly supplied from this 11 kV switchboard. Separate feeders for the auxiliary supply transformer will also 
be fed from this switchboard. 
A separate 220/33 kV 30 MVA transformer will be installed for TANESCO. 
The 11 kV system will be impedance earthed at the transformer 11 kV star-point through a neutral earthing 
resistor. This will ensure adequate design of the plant earthing system for compliance with step and touch 
potentials. 
18.6.5 ELECTRICAL DISTRIBUTION 
The electrical system for the Project is based on an 11 kV high voltage distribution system; 400 V drive voltage 
in the plant, raw water abstraction pumps and decant return pumps; and 400 V supply to the mine services 
area and camp. The system frequency is designed at 50 Hz. 
The main 11 kV switchboard will be located outside of the plant on the northern side of the process plant 
site with incoming supply cabling installed on ladder from the 220/11 kV switchyard and outgoing feeders 
installed in underground conduits to plant and infrastructure loads. 
The main site 11 kV switchboard will supply the process plant 11 kV switchboard via a dedicated feeder. An 
11 kV overhead powerline will feed the external infrastructure. An overhead powerline will reticulate power 
along the northern edge of the plant to the mine services area, main camp, explosive magazine, and 
continues to the raw water abstraction pumping station, with a spur to the decant return pump station. The 
overhead lines will be strung with optical ground wire (OPGW) to facilitate connection of remote facilities via 
fibre optic. 
The plant 11 kV switchboard will supply power to the SAG and ball mills, the mill discharge pumps, and the 
plant 11/0.4 kV transformers. 
18.6.6 EMERGENCY POWER GENERATION 
To prevent equipment damage and extended downtime following power outages, critical site drives and 
feeders have been identified in the load list as essential services. Within the process plant, this includes 
agitators (including CIL tanks), thickener s, the process control system and all lighting and small power. 
Infrastructure such as administration buildings, workshops, CCTV and security have also been included in this 
allowance.

286 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
Emergency generation capacity will be installed consisting of a series of 2,000 kVA (standby rated) high speed 
generators connected at the plant 11 kV switchboard. The system will detect an outage in mains supply and 
automatically restore limited power at 11  kV to the site distribution network. Provision for additional 
generator units has been made. The generators will be supplied by a local gravity fed fuel system with 
capacity for 24 hours run time. 
Perseus is currently conducting a study considering a full-capacity power station located adjacent to the 
220 kV switchyard. This study will evaluate meeting the process  plant's peak demand through the 
deployment of high-speed generators connected to the 11 kV switchboard on-site. The concept will consider 
operation in parallel with the grid supply, accommodating both reduced load conditions and total outages. 
This configuration will allow for seamless transitions between grid and station power without experiencing 
a total blackout. 
In the event of a grid supply failure, the conceptual full-capacity backup power station will be equipped with 
an automated detection system that will restore full power to the site distribution network at 11  kV. The 
generator setup will follow an N+1 redundancy model, ensuring that total demand can be met even in the 
case of a unit failure. 
Perseus is also considering renewable energy options as part of the backup power strategy. 
A full-capacity backup power station is not included in the capital cost estimate presented in Section 21.1.

18.9.1 TAILINGS CHARACTERISATION 
Two cyanidation tailings samples (solids and associated process liquor) were generated by SGS from bulk 
cyanidation tests on the Nyanzaga deposit oxide bulk engineering composite and the Nyanzaga deposit fresh 
bulk engineering composite, as described in Section 13.2.6.9. 
Tailings characterisation testing (Knight Piésold, 2017a) indicates that oxide tailings solids are a non-plastic 
silt with sand, and fresh tailings solids are a low plasticity silt with trace sand. The expected supernatant 
release from 57-58% w/w solids content tailings slurry is in the range of 39-44% of the water in slurry. An 
underdrainage recovery rate between 5% and 10% is expected. A settled tailings density of 1.4 t/m3 to 
1.6 t/m3 is expected in the facility. 
Tailings geochemical tests (Knight Piésold, 2017b) indicate that oxide tailings will be potentially acid forming 
(low capacity), but the subsequent deposition of fresh tailings, characterised as acid consuming, should result 
in excess alkalinity within the TSF. 
The testing reported a moderate number of elemental enrichments, with arsenic and antimony characterised 
as highly enriched (in terms of geochemical abundance indices) and silver, boron and mercury significantly 
enriched. This finding aligns with the head grade observations from metallurgical test work programs, as 
described in Section 13.2.2. Molybdenum enrichment varied from significant in the oxide material to high in 
the fresh material. Sulfur enrichment varied from high in the fresh material to slightly in the oxide material. 
Geochemistry of the tailings supernatant samples was found to be of a poor quality with several metals 
detected at elevated concentrations when compared to Tanzanian guidelines for municipal and industrial 
effluent and drinking water standards. 
18.9.2 GEOTECHNICAL INVESTIGATIONS 
A number of geotechnical investigations have been undertaken at the TSF site between 2017 and 2024  
(Knight Piésold, 2025e). Geotechnical investigations for the TSF comprised test pits across the full internal 
storage area, borehole drilling, field testing, sampling , and laboratory testing . Investigations were also 
undertaken to determine the available construction materials and inform the embankment and foundation 
design. 
A high-level summary of the TSF area ground conditions is as follows: 
• The TSF basin area comprises colluvium/alluvium predominantly clay/silt materials observed to depths 
ranging from 0.0 m to 2.1 m. The valley sides are predominantly colluvium comprising gravel with silt and 
clay exhibiting medium-dense to dense consistency, to depths up to 2.6 m. 
• A high plasticity silt/clay alluvium is present towards the centre of the valley which tends to be black, 
becoming brown and grey. 
• The ground conditions below the colluvium/alluvium typically comprise residual soil with consistency 
varying from very stiff to hard, transitioning to weathered rock. The weathered rock is typically extremely 
weathered with parent rock structure evident. 
 
The investigations indicated that the foundations were suitable for construction of the TSF embankments. 
Any unsuitable material will be removed from the foundation during construction as directed by the site 
engineer. It is expected that structural fill for the embankments will be primarily sourced from mine waste 
rock. 
18.9.3 TAILINGS STORAGE FACILITY DESIGN 
The TSF will be located south of the open pit and will be constructed as a single cell storage facility consisting 
of a multi -zoned earthfill downstream constructed embankment designed to store the LOM processing 
production profile of tailings, as indicated in Figure 17-3. The total footprint area (including the basin area)

292 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
will be approximately 130 ha for Stage 1 of the TSF, increasing to approximately 225 ha for the final stage of 
the TSF. The facility will be constructed as a paddock type storage facility utilising natural ridges to reduce 
the volume of embankment fill, and the waste dump to buttress the northern embankment. 
Given that the cyanidation process leads to the presence of cyanide, cyanide complexes and dissolved metals 
in tailings supernatant, and the geochemistry of the tailings as described in Section 18.9.1, the full internal 
basin area and upstream batter slopes of embankments will be fully lined with HDPE liner. 
The TSF embankment footprint and internal storage area will be cleared, grubbed and topsoil stripped. A 
compacted soil liner (CSL) will be constructed in the TSF basin area, comprising either reworked in -situ 
material or imported low permeability material. All embankment materials will be moisture conditioned and 
compacted in accordance with site specific QAQC requirements, which will be verified by the site engineer. 
An underdrainage system will be installed over the HDPE liner and beneath deposited tailings to reduce the 
pressure head acting on the geomembrane liner, reduce seepage, and improve the geotechnical stability of 
the embankments. The underdrainage system will drain by gravity to collection sumps located at the lowest 
points in the basin. Solution recovered from the underdrainage system will be released to the top of the 
deposited tailings and will report to the supernatant pond. 
A leakage collection and recovery system (LCRS) will be installed beneath the compacted soil liner. Solution 
recovered from the LCRS will be released to the top of the deposited tailings and will report to the 
supernatant pond. 
The TSF will be designed with sufficient capacity and freeboard to completely contain design storm events. 
ANCOLD criteria have been adopted for pond freeboard over the Tanzanian Dam Safety Guidelines, as the 
freeboard requirements of ANCOLD are more stringent. 
An emergency spillway will be constructed for each stage to protect the embankments from overtopping. 
Under normal operating conditions, the available stormwater storage capacity will be in excess of the design 
storm event and therefore no discharge is expected throughout the life of the facility, provided that the TSF 
is managed in accordance with standard operating procedures. 
Tailings will be discharged into the TSF by sub-aerial deposition methods, using multiple spigots at regular 
intervals along the southern perimeter. Tailings will be deposited following the deposition plan, developed 
to locate the supernatant pond towards the decant area in the northern part of the facility and away from 
the embankments. 
A bunded and lined corridor will be constructed for both the tailings delivery pipeline and decant return 
pipeline between the process plant and TSF to contain any spills. Supernatant water will be removed from 
the TSF by a decant pumping system with a turret intake. The turret system acts as a floating water intake 
device that can operate at relatively shallow pond depths. Water drawn from the turret will be pumped back 
to the process water pond at the process plant for reuse. During the early stages of operation, when the risk 
of water shortages is highest, the deposition plan will be managed to improve water recovery. 
The TSF will be raised annually using the downstream method of construction. Raising annually will allow 
designs to be updated based on actual performance and up-to-date mine planning. TSF construction will be 
integrated with the mine waste schedule where possible. The HDPE liner will be extended and spillway raises 
conducted as a part of annual TSF raises. 
18.9.4 TSF DAM BREACH ASSESSMENT 
A preliminary TSF consequence assessment was undertaken in accordance with the requirements of ANCOLD 
guidelines, the GISTM and the Tanzanian Dam Safety Guidelines (Knight Piésold, 2025b). 
The assessment analysed both “sunny day failure” (normal conditions) and “flood failure” (extreme flooding 
conditions). The sunny day failure condition considers when the supernatant pond is operating under typical 
or average conditions. The flood failure conditions consider a scenario where failure occurs during a flood 
event, therefore account ing for coincidental flooding of external catchment areas and assessed the

293 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
incremental impacts of a dam failure under these conditions. The assessment was undertaken assuming 
failure without considering the likelihood or probability of the failure. 
The failure of the TSF was modelled at the final embankment height and full capacity, where the potential 
for volumetric outflow is the highest and inundation area the greatest. 
The TSF has the following ratings based on current guidelines: 
• An ANCOLD Dam Failure Consequence Category of High C for breaches resulting from flooding , and 
Extreme for all other failure modes. 
• A GISTM Dam Failure Consequence Category of Extreme. 
• A rating of Very High A, per the Tanzanian Dam Safety Guideline. 
 
The consequence categories and classifications were used to determine the design criteria for pond storage 
and freeboard conditions, spillway requirements, seismic loading, and factors of safety for stability. 
18.9.5 MONITORING AND SURVEILLANCE 
A monitoring and surveillance program will be developed for the TSF to allow for the safety and performance 
of the TSF to be verified against the design assumptions. The monitoring and surveillance program will allow 
for early identification and mitigation of any potential issues. The surveillance program will include routine 
(daily) TSF safety inspections  and regular TSF reviews by management. The monitoring programme will 
include groundwater monitoring bores and surface water sampling stations to monitor water quality, 
piezometers within the embankments and foundations  to monitor the phreatic surface , and survey 
monitoring of embankment crests to monitor embankment movements. 
18.9.6 CLOSURE 
At the end of the TSF operation, the external embankments will be shaped to be stable under both normal 
and seismic loading conditions, to provide a stable drainage system, and allow for revegetation. 
The TSF closure cover capping is envisaged to comprise a waste rock layer, a low permeability fill layer, and 
a topsoil cover to form a water shedding landform. The closure cover for the tailings surface will be confirmed 
during operations based on ongoing operational tailings geochemistry test results and closure cover system 
trials. 
A closure spillway will be constructed to allow rainfall run -off from the finished surface and to minimise 
ponding of rainfall on the facility post -closure. The closure spillway will allow conveyance of PMP storm 
events without any attenuation. 
18.10 SURFACE WATER AND SEDIMENT MANAGEMENT 
A sediment control and surface water management plan has been developed for the Project (Knight Piésold, 
2025c). The technical assessment considered rainfall events, topography, ground conditions and other 
environmental factors and was based on the ultimate extent of key infrastructure such as the pit, waste 
dumps and the TSF. 
Surface water management will be separated into three categories: 
• Clean water diversions (CWDs) that will divert clean water away from the site to minimise sediment 
control dam (SCD) size. 
• Mine wa ste diversions (MWDs) that will collect c ontaminated runoff from the  mineralised waste 
stockpile, reporting to a specific SCD called the contact water control pond. 
• Sediment laden water diversions (SWDs) that will report to one of three remaining SCDs.

TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
The contact water control pond and other SCDs are shown in Figure 18-1. The SCDs are designed to reduce 
flow velocities to promote sediment settling and mitigate the following: 
• Adverse effect on the quality of water , e.g., increased turbidity, contaminants and nutrients flowing 
downstream. 
• Impacts to flora and fauna and their habitat by filling in deep holes and pools, impacting wetlands and 
aquatic vegetation and exacerbating flooding. 
 
Diversion channels have generally been designed to convey the critical duration of 50 -year average 
recurrence interval (ARI) storm event off the mine site area into the natural drainage pathway or a SCD. The 
SCDs are designed to manage sediment for a 2-year ARI event, with spillways capable of conveying a 100-
year ARI event. 
As part of the  surface water management strategy, culvert crossings have been identified based on the 
proposed internal road alignments. Sizing and quantities of culverts are to be confirmed during detailed 
design. 
The earthworks and drainage design of the process plant facility ensures that any chemically contaminated 
water and process spillage will be contained in bunded areas or the event pond within the plant site. 
The design of these facilities will be finalised in parallel with the broader site infrastructure design.

An Environmental and Social Impact Assessment ( ESIA) was undertaken and submitted to the National

issued by the NEMC is a mandatory legal document that authorises a developer to commence a project after 
successfully completing an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). 
Since the granting of the original EC in 2018, additional studies and engineering works were undertaken by 
OreCorp via their subsidiary SMCL as part of the Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) on the Project. As a result 
of changes in the site layout, SMCL submitted an updated Environmental and Social Management Plan 
(ESMP, (Sotta Mining Corporation Limited, 2023)) to NEMC in July 2023, as per requirements. 
With Perseus’s acquisition of the project and update to the proposed mining methods and site layout, an 
updated ESMP is currently being developed incorporating the results of various associated studies. Once 
complete, this will be submitted to the NEMC  for approval. Perseus does not expect any delays  or 
impediments to receiving this approval. 
In late 2021, the project commenced a detailed Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) planning process (Digby 
Wells Environmental, 2021) which contains an accurate delineation of affected landholdings, details of 
eligibility criteria, proposed compensation and measures to mitigate the impacts of resettlement as per the 
requirements of Section 52 of the Mining Act. The surveys and studies to support the RAP were completed 
in February 2023. Additional details on the RAP can be found in Section 20.10. 
Although several environmental and social impacts have been identified, it is expected that these will be 
successfully mitigated through implementation of a range of measures. Concurrently, there are a number of 
positive impacts expected  as a result of the Project , mainly related to community development and 
opportunities for local community members. 
Part XIV of t he Mining Regulations (2010) relates to Reclamation Requirements, Rehabilitation Bond and 
Mine Closure. Regulation 206 stipulates the requirement for preparation of a Mine Closure Plan (MCP), with 
a conceptual mine closure plan prepared and submitted as part of the ESIA. Regulation 196 requires 
continuous site rehabilitation during the life of the Project and prior to closure, while Regulation 204 requires 
that a post-operational state of mine facilities and post-operational monitoring plan to be submitted to the 
Commissioner of Minerals and the Minister responsible for environment prior to closure. Furthermore, 
Regulation 207 provides guidance for provision of adequate financial assurance for mine closure by the 
holder of a special mining license or mining license.  
A detailed MCP will be required to be submitted to Ministry of Minerals for approval, with updates required

20.4 WATER MANAGEMENT 
20.4.1 SURFACE WATER 
The Wingi River and Lake Victoria are the most dependable water sources for communities , both for 
domestic and agricultural purposes. 
As described in Section 17.8, water for the Project will be sourced from recycle streams within the process 
plant, from the TSF decant, pit dewatering, and abstracted from Lake Victoria. Water requirements will vary 
over the life of the mine. Further, as described in Section 18.10, surface water and sediment management 
infrastructure has been designed to manage and/or contain surface water from the SML footprint, reduce 
flow velocities to promote sediment settling, mitigate adverse effects on water quality, and mitigate impacts 
to flora, fauna and habitat. 
A network of surface water monitoring sites has been established across the SML area. Quarterly water 
quality monitoring has commenced and will continue throughout the life of the Project. A site water 
management plan was developed based on the framework ESMP provided within the Project ESIA document 
(MTL Consulting, 2017). This will be revised based on additional studies being undertaken and will thereafter 
be revised and implemented accordingly. 
20.4.2 GROUNDWATER 
AQ2 Pty Ltd has conducted site investigations , studies,  and hydrogeological modelling to understand 
groundwater in the vicinity of the Nyanzaga Gold Project (AQ2, 2025). AQ2 has determined that the Project 
area is characterised by three aquifers, namely: 
• A shallow perched aquifer formed in ferricrete with groundwater measurement ranging from 0 to 6  
metres below ground level (mbgl), and commonly less than 2 mbgl. 
• A saprock transition zone aquifer with groundwater measurement ranging from 10 to 70 mbgl, varying 
with topographic location both in relation to Nyanzaga Hill and position in the catchment. 
• A variable aquifer formed in the fractured basement, which is discontinuous and of limited areal extent, 
controlled by the presence of fracture zones. Groundwater samples were collected from newly 
constructed monitoring boreholes, hand dug wells, community water supply boreholes and springs.  
 
Groundwater in the Nyanzaga region is generally fresh to brackish with total dissolved solids (TDS) ranging 
from less than 400 mg/L (in the SML) to 1,200 to 1,800 mg/L in the regional monitoring bores. Groundwater 
samples with relatively high TDS come from the saprock aquifer and are characterised by very high 
concentrations of sulfate and bicarbonate.

302 
TECHNICAL REPORT  
 
A numerical groundwater model, based on AQ’s 2022 conceptual hydrogeological model, has been used to 
assess dewatering requirements and potential groundwater impacts associated with the current mine plan. 
Over the open pit mining duration , groundwater inflow rates are predicted to peak at approximately 
1,300 kL/d in year four and then decline to between 900 kL/d and 1,000 kL/d in the final years of mining. 
At the end of mining, dewatering will cease and the mined-out void will refill with inflowing groundwater and 
rainfall recharge. Groundwater levels will recover until a balance is reached between groundwater inflows 
and evaporative losses (from the pit lake surface) and outflows from the pit. 
Following the cessation of mining, a permanent pit lake is predicted to form in the deeper part of the 
Nyanzaga Pit, whilst in the vicinity of the Kilimani deposit, long term groundwater levels are predicted to 
remain below the pit base with no groundwater inflow and only temporary surface waterflooding. The model 
predictions indicate that the final Nyanzaga pit void lake will be a throughflow type system with groundwater 
inflow to the pit void lake from upstream (northeast) and groundwater outflow to downstream (southwest). 
It is recognised that further work is required during 2025, primarily to: 
• Incorporate the structural setting after an update to the geological interpretation into the ground water 
modelling.  
• Undertake pit void water balance modelling to further assess the rates of potential groundwater outflow 
from pit lake after the cessation of mining. 
• Predict the pit lake water quality after cessation of mining.

Mining activities can have a significant impact on the land capability and soil structures because of 
compaction, erosion and land disturbance. During the construction and operation of the mine, actions will

• The current nursery will be upgraded, and seedlings will be planted as part of progressive rehabilitation.

20.10 RESETTLEMENT 
20.10.1 RESETTLEMENT ACTION PLAN (RAP) 
The Nyanzaga Gold Project will cause both physical and economic displacement in the villages of Sotta and 
Nyabila. A Resettlement Action Plan (RAP) is being implemented to support those affected.  
The RAP aims to ensure affected people are compensated fairly and supported to restore or improve their 
livelihoods and living standards. Key elements of the RAP are as follows: 
• The RAP follows Tanzanian law (Land Act 1999, Mining Act 2017) and international standards (IFC 
Performance Standard 5) to ensure fair and transparent resettlement and compensation. 
• Compensation will be at full replacement cost, ensuring replacement land and housing is of equal value 
and quality to what is lost. 
• A valuation report, compliant with Tanzanian law and international standards, will be approved by the 
Chief Valuer. 
• Compensation options include: 
• In-kind compensation (replacement of homes, land, and other lost assets). 
• Cash compensation. 
 
All affected households, whether physically or economically displaced, can participate in a livelihood 
restoration program tailored to their level of impact. A Resettlement Working Group (RWG) was established 
in February 2022  and includes company, government, and community representatives  which leads 
stakeholder engagement and decision-making. A grievance mechanism is in place, allowing affected persons 
to submit complaints or claims free of charge, with guaranteed timely responses. 
20.10.2 RESETTLEMENT PROGRAM 
Surveys and studies to support the RAP were completed in February 2023. The Project has since advanced 
the RAP with compensation payments completed for over 93% of the project affected persons. A housing 
relocation construction program is underway, and the scheduling of house builds will be sequenced to ensure 
that areas of the SML are available to achieve Project development scope and schedule.

This component represents pre-fabricated, pre-assembled, off-the-shelf types of mechanical or electrical

excluding delivery to site (unless otherwise stated ), although does include operating and maintenance

estimate. 
21.1.2.3.3 INSTALLATION 
This component represents the cost to install the plant equipment and bulk materials on site or to perform 
site activities. Installation costs are further divided between trade labour, equipment and contractors’ 
distributables. 
The labour component reflects the cost of the trade labour workforce (excluding management, supervision 
and other onsite support staff) required to construct the Project scope. The labour cost is the product of the 
estimated work hours spent on site multiplied by the cost of labour to the contractor inclusive of overtime 
premiums, statutory overheads, and payroll burden and contractor margin. 
The equipment component reflects the cost of the construction equipment and running costs required to 
construct the Project. The equipment cost includes small tools, consumables, PPE , and the applicable 
contractor’s margin. 
Contractors’ distributable costs encompass the remaining cost of installation and include items such as off-
site management, onsite staff and supervision above trade level, site facilities, cranes (up to 100 t) and crane 
drivers, mobile equipment, scaffold, mobilisation and demobilisation, R&R  breaks, meals and 
accommodation costs, general duration costs, and the applicable contractors’ margin.

Contingency has been applied to the estimate as a deterministic assessment by assessing the level of 
confidence in each of the defining inputs to the item cost being engineering, estimate basis, and vendor or 
contractor information. It should be noted that contingency is not a function of the specified estimate 
accuracy and should be measured against the Project total that includes contingency.

closure capital.
